docs.title: The tower that decides who gets in.
docs.text:
An identity provider for the Symfony ecosystem. On the map of a Symfony application the interface is Symfony, the API is API Platform, and the identity provider is always somewhere else. Beffroi paints that last box the same colour as the other two.

Get started What is Beffroi?

docs.title: What it will not do
docs.text:
Secure by default means there is no option to do it wrong: no implicit flow, no password grant, PKCE with S256 only, redirect URIs compared exactly, iss in every authorization response. Those are properties of the code, not settings of a file.

docs.title: The standalone application
docs.text:
beffroi/op is a provider you deploy rather than a provider you assemble: a Symfony skeleton on the bundle, served by FrankenPHP in worker mode, with PostgreSQL for the model and a broker for the writes the protocol does not wait on.

It is the deployment the project supports, and the one the conformance plans are run against, so a profile reported green is green on this application.

docs.title: Why there is one at all
docs.text: The bundle alone leaves a dozen decisions to whoever installs it: the web server, the worker, the broker, the key management client, the migrations, the two planes, the images. Those decisions are the same for almost everybody, so the project makes them once, in an application, instead of writing them again in a guide. A team that wants to make them differently still can: the bundle is the same bundle.

docs.text:
Page What it covers Deployment The image, FrankenPHP in worker mode, and the two planes Configuration The environment the application reads, and what each variable decides Operating it Rotating keys, rewrapping data keys, migrations, backups Observability What the provider records of a request, a session and a token

It is the apps/op directory of the monorepo, mirrored read only as beffroi-auth/op. It resolves the packages from the directories beside it, so it installs nothing on its own: it is worked on inside the monorepo, and deployed from an image built there rather than from a clone of its mirror.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
What changes from one machine to the next is an environment variable: the issuer, the key management service, the database, the broker, the lifetimes, the host that asks for a client certificate. What the deployment is, its clients, its look, the protocols it turns on, is written in its configuration files.

apps/op/.env holds the values of the development stack, and the production image compiles it with composer dump-env prod, together with a .env.local when the checkout it is built from holds one. A real environment variable wins over both, which is how a deployment says its own. .env carries no secret of a deployment: the key management service, the key it seals under and the secrets of the clients are empty there, and the database and the broker are those of the development stack. That stack writes its own secrets into .env.local, which is never committed and which an image is built without.

docs.title: The provider
docs.text:
Variable In .env What it decides BEFFROI_ISSUER https://op.localhost The issuer of the tenant (OIDC Discovery 1.0 §3), which every token names and every client compares byte for byte: an absolute https URL with no query, no fragment and no trailing slash, plain HTTP on a loopback host only. The application imports the routes of the bundle at the root, so its issuer is an origin with no path. A tenant keeps the issuer its row was written with: beffroi:tenant:synchronize refuses another BEFFROI_KMS_DSN empty The key management service that seals the keys of the tenant, its pairwise salt and its data keys, as the DSN of the client op of config/packages/key_management.yaml. The backends are below BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID empty The master key of that service the tenant is sealed under. {tenant} in it stands for the slug of the tenant, one master key per tenant BEFFROI_KMS_DSN_SECOND empty A second client, second, holding a key under the same identifier, for a run that moves the data keys from one to the other. Empty, the client is declared and never built BEFFROI_PLANE all The plane this process serves: all, interaction or protocol. A route of a plane the process does not serve answers 404 BEFFROI_MTLS_ORIGIN https://mtls.op.localhost The origin of the host that asks for a client certificate, announced in mtls_endpoint_aliases (RFC 8705 §5). Empty, the discovery document announces no alias, which is what a deployment serving one host sets BEFFROI_JWKS_MAX_AGE 300 How long, in seconds, a relying party may cache the JWK Set (RFC 7517 §5). A key staged by a rotation, the SAML signing key aside, is published for this long plus sixty seconds before it takes over, 360 seconds with this value BEFFROI_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL 600 The lifetime of an access token in seconds, whether it is an at+jwt or an opaque reference BEFFROI_ID_TOKEN_TTL 600 The lifetime of an ID token in seconds GEOIP_LICENSE_KEY empty The licence key of the MaxMind account the GeoLite2 databases are downloaded under. Empty, nothing is downloaded, and every session and every act says an address and no place BEFFROI_BREACHED_PASSWORDS_ENDPOINT empty The range endpoint a password is compared against before it is written (NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2): https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/, where the first five hexadecimal characters of the SHA-1 of a password leave and the rest is compared locally. Empty, nobody is asked, and passwords are posed on the rules of the core alone

Each of these is read when the kernel needs it and not when its container is compiled, so changing one asks for a restart of the processes and not for a new image.

docs.title: Symfony, the database and the broker
docs.text:
Variable In .env What it decides APP_ENV dev The environment of the kernel. The production image sets prod APP_SECRET empty The secret of the kernel, framework.secret. .env.dev and .env.test give one each, for their own environment, so a production environment names its own APP_SHARE_DIR var/share The share directory of Symfony, one per environment beneath it, var/share/prod for a production kernel. It holds the filesystem pool of cache.app, and with it the caches of the bundle DEFAULT_URI https://op.localhost The URL Symfony generates absolute URLs under outside a request, framework.router.default_uri DEFAULT_LOCALE en The language a page falls back to, among the two the application serves, en and fr DATABASE_URL postgresql://beffroi:beffroi@127.0.0.1:5432/beffroi?serverVersion=16&charset=utf8 The PostgreSQL database. The entrypoint of the image waits for it, and the migrations refuse any other platform MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN amqp://beffroi:beffroi@localhost:5672/%2f/messages The broker of the four lanes. Each lane names an exchange and a queue, which only an AMQP transport takes, so this is an amqp:// DSN. The failure transport stays in the database SYMFONY_TRUSTED_PROXIES not set The proxies whose forwarded address Symfony reads, framework.trusted_proxies. The application names none

The bundle reads its own default for the lanes, BEFFROI_MESSENGER_DSN, only where an application declares no transport of the same name. This one declares all four, so that variable is not read here.

docs.title: The web server
docs.text:
These are read by Caddy and FrankenPHP, not by the kernel.

Variable What it decides SERVER_NAME The host Caddy serves the provider on, localhost when it is not set MTLS_SERVER_NAME The host of the listener that asks for a client certificate, in mtls.Caddyfile CADDY_EXTRA_CONFIG Configuration added to the Caddyfile beside the site of SERVER_NAME. import mtls.Caddyfile is what serves the host that asks for a client certificate CADDY_GLOBAL_OPTIONS Directives added to the global options of the Caddyfile CADDY_SERVER_EXTRA_DIRECTIVES Directives added to the site of SERVER_NAME, such as a tls directive naming a certificate and its key CADDY_SERVER_LOG_OPTIONS Directives added to the log block of each site FRANKENPHP_CONFIG Directives of the frankenphp block. The production image sets import worker.Caddyfile, which is worker mode FRANKENPHP_WORKER_CONFIG Directives added to the worker block: the watch lines of the development stack, nothing in production

docs.title: The key management service
docs.text:
The DSN and the key identifier are what change from one backend to the next: the code and the envelope are the same. An envelope sealed by one backend does not open with another.

SodiumA fileHashiCorp VaultAWS KMS

A key inline in the environment, which is what the development stack provisions.

BEFFROI_KMS_DSN="sodium://?keys[signing]=<32 bytes, base64url>"
BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID="signing"

Whoever reads the environment of the process holds the master key.

The same sodium key read from a file of its own, one per tenant, outside the web root and outside the sealed keys: it holds against a dump of the storage, not against a compromise of the host.

BEFFROI_KMS_DSN="sodium+dir:///app/var/kms?ext=.key"
BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID="beffroi-{tenant}"

The file of the tenant default is /app/var/kms/beffroi-default.key: thirty-two bytes and nothing else, mode 0600 in a directory 0700, which the development stack writes this way when it is missing:

umask 077 && mkdir -p /app/var/kms && chmod 700 /app/var/kms && head -c 32 /dev/urandom > /app/var/kms/beffroi-default.key

The Transit engine wraps the data key of every envelope, and the private key never reaches Vault.

BEFFROI_KMS_DSN="hashicorp-vault-transit://<token>@<host>:8200"
BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID="beffroi-{tenant}"

The Transit key of a tenant is beffroi-<slug>, of type aes256-gcm96 and created with derived=true: the envelope carries a context that binds it to its tenant, Vault honours a context on a derived key only, and the bridge refuses to seal under a key that is not one. The development stack also creates it not exportable, with no plaintext backup, and refuses its deletion. The token needs three paths and nothing else:

path "transit/datakey/plaintext/beffroi-*" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
}

path "transit/decrypt/beffroi-*" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
}

path "transit/keys/beffroi-*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

The Vault of the development stack is a dev server answering over plain HTTP, which its DSN says with ?scheme=http.

A symmetric key of the account wraps the data key of every envelope.

BEFFROI_KMS_DSN="aws-kms://default?region=<region>"
BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID="alias/beffroi-{tenant}"

The credentials come from the DSN or from the provider chain of async-aws, and any host other than default in the DSN is a custom endpoint. The key of a tenant is a SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT key for ENCRYPT_DECRYPT, behind the alias alias/beffroi-<slug>, so a new key behind the same alias changes nothing in the configuration.

docs.title: What the files say
docs.text:
The configuration files are compiled into the container of the kernel when the image is built, so a change to them reaches a deployment with a new image. Outside the development environment, config/packages/beffroi.yaml says this:

Section What the application writes What it means for a deployment tenant.look The logo at /tenant-logo.svg, a placeholder served from the issuer, and the colours #1f6feb on #ffffff The mark and the colours of the tenant, on every page. A logo served from another host needs that origin in the img-src of config/packages/nelmio_security.yaml, and the host to answer Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin, the pages of the account requiring it tenant.self_served_claims Fourteen claims of OIDC Core §5.1, from name to phone_number What a person may change of themselves on the page of their account. A tenant whose directory owns the data names none web_push.subject mailto:operator@op.localhost Naming a subject turns web push on (RFC 8292 §2.1): a mailto: or https: URI at which a push service reaches the operator. Without the section, no push leaves the deployment saml.identity_provider Requests signed, a key staged for seven days and working for a year, metadata cached for a day The tenant is a SAML identity provider and serves its metadata at /saml/metadata. Without the section, it draws no SAML key and serves no metadata tokens Codes for 60 seconds; refresh tokens for thirty days and ninety days at most from the authorization, the thirty days renewed at each rotation of the tokens that rotate, those of a public client bound to no key or certificate The lifetimes the environment does not carry clients None The clients of the deployment, declared as your first client is

The application writes no client_registration outside development, so its tenant has no registration endpoint. Everything else keeps the defaults of the bundle: an act of the journal and a change of a record are kept 180 days, an origin may send 2400 requests a minute and an authenticated client 1200.

The whole configuration tree

docs.title: What only development reads
docs.text: The blocks under when@dev declare what the development stack needs and nothing a deployment does: the clients of the OpenID conformance suite and of the demonstrations, an open registration endpoint for the Dynamic OP plan, a SAML service provider with the peers it is judged by, and an issuer of assertions it trusts. Their variables are read in the development environment: BEFFROI_REGISTRATION_MODE, the CONFORMANCE_*, OIDC_DEMO_* and DEMO_* secrets and key sets, BEFFROI_DEV_USER_SUBJECT, BEFFROI_DEMO_HOST_IP, APP_PROFILER and VAR_DUMPER_SERVER. The demonstration of the flows is wired in the test environment of the application's own suite as well, so three of them are read there too, DEMO_SERVICE_SECRET, DEMO_CIBA_POLL_SECRET and BEFFROI_DEV_USER_SUBJECT, which .env.test gives as fixtures. A production kernel reads none of them.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: One image runs two kinds of process: the HTTP server, FrankenPHP in worker mode inside the Caddy server it is built on, and the worker, which consumes the lanes of Messenger and the schedule of the timed steps. Beside them the provider needs PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ and a key management service.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
apps/op/Dockerfile builds on dunglas/frankenphp:1-php8.5 and adds the extensions the provider needs: apcu, intl, opcache, zip, pdo_pgsql, amqp, gmp, sodium and uuid. Its build context is the root of the monorepo, because the application installs the packages beside it through path repositories.

Stage What it is frankenphp_base The extensions, the PHP settings of the application, the entrypoint and the Caddy configuration frankenphp_dev The development image, into which the stack mounts the monorepo, running FrankenPHP with --watch frankenphp_prod The production image: the packages are copied to /src and the application to /app, installed without the development dependencies, with an authoritative class map, .env and any .env.local beside it compiled for production, the stylesheet built and the assets compiled 
docker build --file apps/op/Dockerfile --target frankenphp_prod .

apps/op/ is copied as the working copy holds it, and composer dump-env prod compiles a .env.local it finds there. The one the development stack writes holds its key management service, the secrets of its clients and the password of its user, so the image is built from a checkout that holds no .env.local.

The production image sets APP_ENV=prod, reads php.ini-production, preloads config/preload.php into OPcache, and turns worker mode on: the kernel is booted once per worker and serves every request that worker takes, so a signing key opened with the key management service stays open in it, and the service is asked once per key and per worker rather than once per signature.

docs.title: The HTTP server
docs.text:
The command of the image is frankenphp run --config /etc/frankenphp/Caddyfile. Before it starts, the entrypoint does two things when .env names a DATABASE_URL, which the one of the application does:

  1. it waits for the database, sixty attempts one second apart, and stops at once on an error it cannot recover from;
  2. it plays the migrations, doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction --all-or-nothing, every time the server starts. The migrations of the bundle are written for PostgreSQL and refuse any other platform.

The health check of the image asks the metrics endpoint of the Caddy admin API inside the container, curl -f http://localhost:2019/metrics, after a start period of sixty seconds.

docs.title: The two planes
docs.text:
Every route of the bundle carries its plane in its name, beffroi_protocol_* for what a client or a resource server calls and beffroi_interaction_* for what a browser reads. BEFFROI_PLANE restricts a process to one of them:

BEFFROI_PLANE What the process serves all Both planes, which is what .env says protocol The protocol plane; every route of the interaction plane answers 404 interaction The interaction plane; every route of the protocol plane answers 404

The refusal comes after the router and before the firewall, so a request to the other plane opens no session and counts against no budget. The root / of the application belongs to the interaction plane, and a route whose name carries no plane, such as /theme, is served by every process. A process serves its plane on each of its hosts, the one that asks for a client certificate included. Whatever sends a request to one process or the other reads its path, and the endpoints give the plane of every path.

docs.title: The worker
docs.text:
The worker is the same image, running the consumer of Messenger on the schedule and the four lanes of the provider, in this order, which is the order it takes them in:

bin/console messenger:consume scheduler_beffroi async_notifications async_priority_high async_priority_medium async_priority_low --time-limit=3600 --memory-limit=256M

Started with bin/console, the entrypoint waits for the database as it does for the server, and plays no migration: the server is the process that migrates, and the development stack starts the worker once the server reports healthy. The consumer stops after an hour, or once it holds 256 MB, and the restart policy of the stack starts it again.

Transport What it carries scheduler_beffroi The clock of the timed steps. One process consumes it: the steps are idempotent, and are not written to run twice at once async_notifications What the provider carries to somebody it does not own: logout tokens (Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.5), the notification that a backchannel request was answered (CIBA Core §10.2), and web push to the browsers of a person (RFC 8030) async_priority_high Nothing the bundle routes async_priority_medium The writes a request does not wait for, and the timed steps the schedule hands over async_priority_low The events of the core and of the protocol, which the journal writes down and the enrichment of a provenance reads

The worker is therefore the one process that calls a client back, and the one that writes the journal. A provider whose worker stops goes on answering requests, and the broker keeps the messages until a worker consumes them.

The lanes are transports of RabbitMQ: each of them names the exchange beffroi_messages and a queue bound to its routing key, options an AMQP transport takes and the Doctrine transport refuses. What fails for good lands in the failure transport, failed, which is a table of the database whatever the broker.

docs.title: What the processes share
docs.text:
The server signs with keys the worker rotates, and the worker enriches with databases the console downloads, so some state has to be the same for all of them.

What Where Written by Read by The sealed keys of the tenant, and its pairwise salt var/keys beffroi:keys:*, the timed step of the key lifecycle, and the first process that needs the salt Every process that signs, decrypts or seals The key of the file backend, when that is the key management service var/kms Whoever provisions it Every process The GeoLite2 databases of addresses var/geoip beffroi:geoip:refresh, the weekly step The worker, which enriches a provenance The FIDO metadata var/webauthn beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh, beffroi:webauthn:mds-import The passkey ceremonies, which check an attestation against it

The development stack gives var/keys, var/kms and var/geoip a volume each, mounted on the server and on the worker alike: a rotation done by one process changes nothing for another that does not see the same directory.

The bundle keeps eight caches in pools of their own, so that a deployment can point them at a shared store without touching the rest of its cache:

Pool What it holds beffroi.client_keys The keys read from the jwks_uri of a client beffroi.issuer_keys The keys read from the jwks_uri of a trusted issuer beffroi.client_assertions The client assertions already seen beffroi.issuer_assertions The assertions of trusted issuers already seen beffroi.software_statements The software statements already seen beffroi.request_objects The request objects already seen beffroi.dpop What DPoP remembers of a proof beffroi.load What each load budget has been asked

Each of them is on cache.app, which the application leaves on the filesystem adapter Symfony gives it, in %kernel.share_dir%/pools/app. The share directory carries the environment, so with the APP_SHARE_DIR of .env the pools of a production kernel are in var/share/prod/pools/app. Two containers share these pools when they share that directory, or once a deployment points the pools at a store they both reach, and each holds its own otherwise. The application names no session handler either, so the session of a browser lives where the native handler of PHP keeps it, in the container that served it.

docs.title: TLS and the two hosts
docs.text:
Caddy terminates TLS for the host of SERVER_NAME. Both hosts of the image use one snippet of its Caddyfile, which is the TLS a FAPI 1.0 plan measures: an RSA key of 2048 bits, and below TLS 1.3 the two suites of FAPI 1.0 Advanced Final §8.5 a listener built on Go can offer, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. TLS 1.2 is the floor Caddy already holds.

The host that asks for a client certificate is a host of its own (RFC 8705 §5). It is served when CADDY_EXTRA_CONFIG imports mtls.Caddyfile, under the name MTLS_SERVER_NAME gives it, and announced to clients through BEFFROI_MTLS_ORIGIN. Its listener asks for a certificate and serves the connection when none is presented, so a client that authenticates another way never fails at the handshake. The ordinary host asks for nothing.

  • The certificate reaches PHP in a server variable, SSL_CLIENT_CERT, and never in a header. A client sets every header of its request and no variable of the process that serves it. A request carrying a certificate in Ssl-Client-Cert, X-Ssl-Client-Cert, X-Client-Cert or X-Forwarded-Client-Cert is refused with invalid_request (RFC 6749 §5.2) at an endpoint that reads a certificate. The TLS connection of that host therefore ends at this listener.
  • Only the leaf reaches PHP, so no chain is validated there. The handshake proves that the client holds the private key of what it presented (RFC 8446 §4.4.3), which is what self_signed_tls_client_auth (RFC 8705 §2.2) needs. A deployment that authenticates clients with tls_client_auth (RFC 8705 §2.1) adds a trust_pool to the client_auth block of mtls.Caddyfile, so the chain is validated at the edge.

The variables of the web server

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text: The address of a request is read by Symfony behind the proxies it trusts, and the application names none: framework.trusted_proxies reads SYMFONY_TRUSTED_PROXIES. That address is what the load budget of an origin is counted under, 2400 requests a minute by default before a 429, and what every session and every act of the journal records as where it came from. Behind a proxy that is not named there, every request has the address of the proxy.

docs.title: The headers
docs.text:
Two layers write the security headers, and where they meet, one gives way. The bundle gives every page of the interaction plane X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, Cache-Control: no-store and the floor of a content policy, frame-ancestors 'none'. The application writes the headers of a deployment on every answer, from two files of its configuration, config/packages/nelmio_security.yaml and config/packages/nelmio_cors.yaml:

  • X-Frame-Options is left as a page already carries it, and Referrer-Policy is written again with the value the pages carry, no-referrer;
  • on a page whose content policy is the floor alone, App\Http\DeploymentPolicyPrevails drops the floor before the policy of the deployment is written, so one policy is sent. A page that computed a whole policy of its own keeps it, the form post response and the front-channel logout page, and so does a redirection.

A header written twice is not replaced, it collides: two content policies are both enforced, and what applies is their intersection. Nothing the application writes is therefore written again in the web server or at the edge. The assets compiled into public/assets/ are answered by FrankenPHP without asking PHP, and carry none of these headers.

The session cookie is the one header of the provider no bundle sets, so the application names it: __Host-beffroi_session, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, on the path / and with no Domain. HSTS is not sent in the development environment, where it would pin every .localhost name of the machine to HTTPS.

The headers

docs.title: What leaves the provider
docs.text:
A deployment that filters what goes out reads it here. No outbound redirect is followed, whoever asks.

From To When Every process The key management service To open a key, a salt or a data key, and to seal one The server The jwks_uri of a client or of a trusted issuer To read its keys, which are then kept a day, and again when an assertion names a key the kept set does not hold The server The request_uri of a client When an authorization request names one The server The sector_identifier_uri of a client When a client registers or replaces itself The server, the console The list of compromised passwords, when one is named When a password is written, and the answer is waited for The worker The list of compromised passwords, when one is named After a login, for a password already posed The worker The backchannel_logout_uri of a client When a session that client signed in ends The worker The backchannel_client_notification_endpoint of a client When a backchannel request in ping mode is answered The worker The push service of a browser When a backchannel request waits on the person who subscribed that browser The worker, the console The metadata of the SAML peers given by URL Every hour, and on beffroi:saml:*:refresh The worker, the console MaxMind, when a licence key is named Every week, and on beffroi:geoip:refresh The console The FIDO Metadata Service On beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Every session and every event carries a request context: an address, a user agent, and what is derived from them, enriched asynchronously so that a sign-in never waits on it. What is recorded, and for how long, is a property of the deployment.

docs.title: The journal
docs.text:
The acts of the provider are written down, kept and read: who did what, when and from where. Nothing turns the journal on; what a deployment configures is how long an act is kept, journal.retention, 180 days by default, which is the duration the CNIL deliberation 2021-122 holds for a log of connections. A deployment under another obligation says its own, and a timed step forgets, once a day, what is past it.

Every event of the core and of the protocols is an act, written under the name the event gives itself: user.authenticated, authentication.failed, tokens.issued, consent.revoked, session.ended, tenant.key_rotated and the others. The worker writes it on the lane the events travel on, so the journal is never on the path of a request, and an act that cannot be written down does not undo what was done.

A row holds what follows and nothing else, no field a caller could fill with a secret:

What How it is kept The name of the act In the clear When it happened In the clear The tenant In the clear Where it came from: the address, the user agent and the place derived from them Sealed under the data key of the tenant, in a family of its own The person it was done in the name of, by the subject their account carries, when it names one In the clear: a subject names a person without saying anything about them The client it concerned, by the identifier it was registered under, when it concerns one In the clear The identifier of the row A UUIDv7, so the journal sorts by time on its primary key

The reads that hand a person over to a third party are acts too: an introspection that tells a resource server who a token names, introspection.answered, and a UserInfo answer, userinfo.answered. An introspection that describes nobody, because the token is inactive or held by a client for itself, writes nothing.

A person reads the acts of their account on the page of their acts. An operator reads them with beffroi:user:journal:

bin/console beffroi:user:journal alice --from=2026-01-01 --to=2026-01-31 --act=tokens.issued --format=json

--from and --to are two days in UTC, both included, --act is repeatable, --client narrows to one application, and --format=json writes the document a request about what happened in somebody's name is answered with. A period that reaches past what the deployment keeps is answered with how long it keeps an act and the day that reaches, never with an empty table that looks complete.

docs.title: Where a request came from
docs.text:
What Where it comes from The address The address of the client as Symfony reads it, behind the proxies SYMFONY_TRUSTED_PROXIES names The user agent The User-Agent header, its surrounding whitespace trimmed and cut at 1024 characters, and none when it is empty The place Derived from the address on the lane of the events, from the GeoLite2 City and ASN databases, and written back on the session that recorded it

A console command records beffroi-console/<command> (<user>@<host>) in place of a user agent, and a timed step beffroi-scheduler/<schedule> (<host>), with no address in either.

A provenance says from where and not only from which address. The databases are read locally: what leaves the provider is a request for a file once a week, carrying the licence key of the deployment and nothing of anybody who signed in. They are published by MaxMind under their own licence, so nothing is shipped and nothing is downloaded without a licence key: a deployment that names none in GEOIP_LICENSE_KEY serves every flow with a provenance that says an address and no place.

docs.title: What a client was given
docs.text:
At each act that hands something over, the provider keeps what left with it: the scopes, the claims asked for by name (OIDC Core §5.5) and the authorization details (RFC 9396 §7), sealed in a family of their own, and the shape of the access token, under the subject of the person, as the journal names them. What an application obtained of somebody therefore still has an answer after the consent it was given under was taken back.

It is kept exactly as long as the act that gave it, and forgotten by the same timed step: an act whose details are gone, or details whose act is gone, would be half an answer.

docs.title: What a record used to say
docs.text: The changes of the claims of a person, what each one said before and after, are kept sealed under the data key of the tenant, under a retention of their own, history.retention, 180 days as well unless the deployment says otherwise, and forgotten by a timed step once a day. A person reads them at /account/profile/changes.

docs.title: The logs
docs.text:
The logs are for failures. In production, Monolog writes JSON to the standard error of the process, in two handlers:

Handler What it writes main Every channel but deprecations, held in a buffer of the fifty latest records and written, with what follows, once one of them is an error. An error that is a 404 or a 405 is not one deprecation The deprecations, as they come

A console command also writes its log lines on its own output, the event and doctrine channels aside. In the development environment every channel but event goes to var/log/dev.log, from debug up.

Besides what Symfony logs of a request or a message that fails, the provider writes these lines of its own:

Level When info A timed step forgot or removed something: acts of the journal and what a client was given at them, changes of a record, expired archives, rows that could no longer do anything, clients that registered themselves and that nobody used. A GeoLite2 database, or the metadata of a SAML peer, was refreshed or found unchanged. A push service answered that a subscription is gone, and the subscription was taken out warning A refresh of the GeoLite2 databases was refused. A database of addresses cannot be read, or answered a record the provider cannot read. A push service did not take a notification. A claim was not sent to a SAML service provider, its value being neither a string, an integer, a boolean nor a list of them error The metadata of a SAML peer were refused, or those of a whole role could not be refreshed. A client that registered itself holds metadata the provider now refuses, and is served as no client

In production an info or a warning reaches the log only beside an error. The acts are in the journal, not in the log.

Caddy writes an access log for each of its sites, one line per request with its path and query string. CADDY_SERVER_LOG_OPTIONS adds directives to both logs. On the site of SERVER_NAME, the authorization parameter of the query is replaced by REDACTED; the site that asks for a client certificate replaces nothing. A path is written as it was requested, the link of an enrolment ticket, /enrol/{ticket}/{value}, included.

docs.title: Metrics and health
docs.text:
The provider exports no metrics of its own. The health check of the image reads the metrics endpoint of the Caddy admin API inside the container, http://localhost:2019/metrics, and the development stack reports its worker healthy while messenger:consume is the first process of its container.

The panel the provider adds to the Symfony profiler is wired only in a kernel that runs in debug, and the web profiler is registered in the development and test environments alone: a production kernel has neither.

docs.title: Operating it
docs.text: A provider is operated, not installed once: keys rotate, data keys are rewrapped, migrations run, backups are taken and restored. Each of those has a command, and each command says what it did. The commands are the console commands of the bundle, run with bin/console in a container of the image, or with castor console on the development stack.

docs.title: At every deployment
docs.text:
1. The migrations are played by the HTTP server each time it starts, before it serves anything. A process that booted before a migration changing the type of a column reads that column with the type it booted with, and a worker runs for an hour, so a migration played by hand is followed by a restart of the server and of the workers. castor console does that on the development stack whenever the command it runs is the migration.
  2. The row of the tenant follows the configuration: beffroi:tenant:synchronize creates it, or writes on it the name, the acr policy, the look and the claims its people may change of themselves that the configuration says, then prints the row. The provider serves nothing while the row and the configuration disagree. A changed issuer is refused: the issuer of a tenant does not change, every token issued so far names it.
  3. Two questions for the pipeline, both of which write nothing and fail when the answer is no: beffroi:keys:list --check opens the keys in use and the ones about to be with the key management service, and fails on one it cannot open or that has worked past its age with nothing staged behind it; beffroi:doctor says whether the deployment holds together, one line per point it looks at.

docs.title: What time does on its own
docs.text:
Some of it is not operated at all, because time does it: one timed step per thing that comes round, handed to the lane of the writes like any other, so a deployment that runs the worker runs them. A step that forgets reads a bounded number of rows and leaves the rest to the next run, and logs a line only when it did something.

Every What it does minute Advances the lifecycle of the keys: stages a successor for a key that has worked its age, activates a staged key whose delay has elapsed, retires a key past its date hour Drops the clients that registered themselves and that nobody uses any more, forgets the archives past their week, drops the rows that can no longer do anything, and reads again the metadata of the SAML service providers and upstream identity providers day Forgets the acts of the journal past their retention, with what a client was given at each, and the changes of a record past theirs week Refreshes the GeoLite2 databases of addresses, which is the cadence MaxMind publishes them at

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
A rotation asks nothing of anybody. A key works for an age, ninety days, or a year for the SAML signing key, and the step of the minute stages its successor; the successor is published for the staging delay, 360 seconds with the values of the application or seven days for the SAML key, then takes over, and the key it replaces stays published while what is bound to it may still arrive.

By hand, the same thing is three commands:

bin/console beffroi:keys:rotate
bin/console beffroi:keys:activate <kid>
bin/console beffroi:keys:retire --due

beffroi:keys:rotate stages a key of the default signature algorithm, or of the one --algorithm names, and says when it takes over. beffroi:keys:activate makes a staged key the active one before its delay has elapsed. --now on the rotation does both at once: a relying party whose copy of the JWK Set is younger than sixty seconds then refuses the new tokens, or encrypts to the old key, until its copy is that old.

docs.title: A compromised key
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:keys:rotate --compromised

The new key takes over at once, and the compromised one leaves the JWK Set with no window: nothing bound to it is honoured from then on. --algorithm names the key when it is not one of the default signature algorithm. A key that is already retiring is taken out of the JWK Set before its date by beffroi:keys:retire <kid> --force.

docs.title: Data keys
docs.text:
Personal data is sealed under a data key per tenant and per family of columns, and the data keys are wrapped by the master key of the tenant.

Command What it does beffroi:data-keys:list Lists the data keys of the tenant by scope, with when each was minted, the master key that wraps it and the key management client that opens it. Reads only, and never opens a key beffroi:data-keys:rewrap --to=<client> Wraps the data keys of the tenant with another client from then on, or with another master key of the same one, --from narrowing it to the keys one client holds and --dry-run listing what would move. No sealed value is read or rewritten, and the master key is derived from BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID rather than asked for beffroi:data-keys:destroy Erases the data keys of the tenant, which makes every personal datum it had sealed unreadable for good. It asks for the slug of the tenant to be typed back, and cannot be undone

The clients of this application are op, which every key of the tenant is sealed with, and second, which is built from BEFFROI_KMS_DSN_SECOND when that variable names one. Nothing schedules a rewrap: a person asks for it.

docs.title: The data downloaded
docs.text: Command When it is run by hand Its timed step beffroi:geoip:refresh The day a licence key is named, and to read why a refresh was refused Every week beffroi:saml:service-provider:refresh, beffroi:saml:identity-provider:refresh For the first reading of a peer just declared, and to read why a document was refused Every hour beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh, beffroi:webauthn:mds-import To fill the FIDO metadata an attestation is checked against None

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text:
beffroi:doctor is what to ask first. It reads, writes nothing, and is safe on a provider serving traffic. What it looks at is what is wired, and in this application that is one point: whether a logout token is retried for as long as it stays verifiable. A deployment that sends the notifications to a transport of its own, retried on another schedule, keeps a provider that works and logout tokens a client may refuse when they arrive late, after a rotation or after the client restarts, which nothing else shows.

A message that fails is tried again, then kept. The three lanes of the provider's own writes retry it on the numbers the bundle prepends; the lane of the notifications retries it on the schedule of the back-channel logout, which is also how long a logout token stays verifiable.

Lanes Retries First wait Multiplier Longest wait async_priority_high, async_priority_medium, async_priority_low 4 1 second 4 30 seconds async_notifications 6 2 seconds 3 60 seconds

What is still failing after that lands in the failure transport, failed, a table of the database. Its body stays sealed there; the class of the message, its stamps and its tenant are in the clear, so that messenger:failed:show names a failed message, dates it and says why without opening it.

A key management service that does not answer is a 503. Wherever a request needed it, the answer is 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 10: nothing was refused to the person, counted against them or forgotten, and the same request is served once the service is back. The outage is an act of the journal, kms.unavailable, with the provenance of the request that met it. The worker does not start without a key management service at all.

A spent load budget is a 429, with a Retry-After and Cache-Control: no-store, and an act of the journal, load.budget_spent.

docs.title: What to back up
docs.text:
One directory to back up, one key management service to lose.

What Where What it holds The database PostgreSQL Everything the model writes, the personal data sealed in their columns, and the data keys wrapped by the master key The sealed keys var/keys One file per key of the tenant, and the pairwise salt of the tenant beside them, each sealed by the key management service The master key The key management service What opens all of the above

No command restores a deployment: a restore is the database and var/keys put back together, under the same master key. The pairwise subjects of OpenID Connect and the persistent identifiers of SAML are computed from the salt and never drawn, so they are the same after a restore that brings the salt back with the database. The GeoLite2 databases in var/geoip and the FIDO metadata in var/webauthn are written again by the commands that wrote them.

docs.title: Index
docs.text: title: Identity core description: What beffroi/core holds: tenants, users, credentials, groups, sessions and keys, in pure PHP.

docs.title: Identity core
docs.text:
beffroi/core is the identity model and nothing else. It knows no protocol, no HTTP, no container and no ORM: no class in it has ever heard of OAuth, of a Request or of Doctrine. What it needs from the outside, it asks for through a port.

That is what makes it testable without a kernel, and what makes the provider's identity model its own rather than borrowed from whatever application hosts it.

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text:
• Tenants

    The unit everything else belongs to. One issuer, one set of keys, one population of users.

  • Users

    A person, their username, their standard claims, the source that created them, and the subject identifier clients know them by.

  • Credentials

    A password, a passkey, a TOTP secret, backup codes. Several per person, each one its own kind.

  • Authentication sessions

    What a person proved, when, and from where. What a grant reads to say acr and auth_time.

  • Groups

    Membership, and where each membership came from: declared here, asserted by an upstream provider, or pushed by a directory.

  • Linked identities

    The same person at an upstream provider, so federation does not duplicate them.

  • Keys

    The signing keys of the tenant, sealed by a key management service, rotated without an outage.

  • Personal data

    Sealed columns, blind indexes, and data keys that can be rewrapped while the provider runs.

docs.title: How it is laid out
docs.text:
Four layers, and the dependencies only ever point inwards.

Layer What is in it What it may depend on Domain The model and its rules. A rule of an entity lives on the entity PHP, PSR interfaces, and the libraries the model is built from Port The interfaces the outside implements: repositories, clock, hashers, key management Domain Application The use cases that orchestrate. One responsibility each, named after what they do: SessionOpener, SessionTerminator, UserProvisioner Domain and Port Bridge The implementations: a password hasher, a TOTP library, an in-memory repository for tests all of the above, and the library it bridges

A static analysis of the dependency graph fails the build when a layer reaches where it is not allowed to, so the rule is not a convention anybody can forget.

docs.title: Adding to it
docs.text:
A new kind of credential, a new password algorithm, a new source of randomness is a class that implements the interface of its capability, tagged in the wiring. It is never a new case in a match, never a new value in an enumeration of kinds, and never a class name read from a string. A kind names itself, and it declares what it can do by the interfaces it implements: a credential that can be revoked implements RevocableCredentialInterface, one identified at an upstream provider implements ExternallyIdentifiedCredentialInterface.

The ports of the core

docs.title: Authentication sessions
docs.text: A session records what was actually proven: which methods, when each one was proven last, from which address and with which user agent. It is the session of the provider and not of a client: one sign-in serves every client of OpenID Connect and every SAML service provider of the tenant the browser goes on to. A grant reads a snapshot of it rather than the live session, which is what makes auth_time, acr and amr mean something at the moment a token was issued and not at the moment it is read.

docs.title: What a session holds
docs.text:
Field What it holds Proofs Each method proven, a value of RFC 8176 §2 or fed, with the instant it was proven last Opened at When the login that opened it ended Expires at Twelve hours after it was opened, or earlier when an upstream identity provider allows less Created from, last seen from The provenance of the request that opened it and of the request of its last proof: when it was received, the address and the user agent, with the place of the address once it is found Ended at, ended by The first end, and who ended it

The identifier of a session is a UUID. It is the sid of the ID tokens, logout tokens and self-contained access tokens issued under it, and the SessionIndex of the SAML assertions written from it, so a logout asked for by either protocol names the same session.

The proofs stay readable in the database, every token issued from the session carrying them anyway; the two provenances are sealed under the data key of the tenant. The place of an address is looked up once the session is opened, on the lane of the events, in the GeoLite2 databases of the deployment and nowhere else: a deployment that holds none keeps an address and no place, and no login waits for it. A later proof writes its provenance as it was received and asks for no lookup of its own.

docs.title: What it proved
docs.text:
amr (RFC 8176 §2) is the list of methods proven, with mfa beside them when two factors of different kinds were proven, a knowledge, a possession or an inherence. Each kind of credential says what one authentication with it proves:

Login Methods A password pwd A password, then a code pwd and otp, so mfa too A passkey bound to its authenticator hwk, user, and mfa when the authenticator verified the user A synced passkey swk, user, and mfa when the authenticator verified the user A sign-in through an upstream identity provider fed, and pwd, sc or otp when its class of authentication means exactly that method

fed is not a value RFC 8176 registers: it is the one Microsoft Entra ID writes for a federated assertion. Signing in through an organisation gives the classes that add a method.

auth_time (OIDC Core §2) is the most recent proof. A session opened by an upstream identity provider dates its proof with the AuthnInstant of the assertion, the instant the person authenticated there, and never later than the moment the response arrived.

acr is never stored. A session satisfies every class of the policy of its tenant whose predicate holds on its proofs, and when nothing asks for a class in particular it answers with the first of them.

docs.title: Opening one
docs.text:
Every login that opens a session ends in the same place, whatever it proved: a password, a password followed by a code, a passkey, an assertion of an upstream identity provider. That place opens the session, writes the act user.authenticated to the journal of the person, and refuses what does not reach the floor of the logins of the tenant: proofs under it open nothing, wherever the login came from, and the refusal is written as a refused login.

A password alone does not sign in a person who holds a second factor. When the person holds an active TOTP, the password the login page verified opens nothing: the login is held in the HTTP session of the browser for five minutes, and the code page asks for a code. A code accepted in time opens the session on pwd and otp, both dated when the code was accepted; past the five minutes, the password is asked again before any code is read.

The browser is bound to it. The HTTP session of the browser holds the identifier of the session, and its own identifier is drawn again at that moment, so a session identifier planted in a browser before the login names nothing afterwards. A browser whose session has ended or expired is treated as a browser that holds none.

docs.title: Proving again
docs.text:
A login on a browser that already holds a session of the same person opens no second session: its proofs are added to the session the browser holds, the newest proof of a method replacing the older one, so auth_time moves to that login and amr grows by what it proved. No user.authenticated is written for it, the act of the credential it used being written as for any login. The expiry of the session is never extended by it, and a sign-in through an upstream identity provider that allows less shortens it. A login of another person on a browser that holds a session ends that session first, and opens a new one.

Something asks for that login:

  • A client, with prompt=login, a max_age the last proof of the session exceeds, an acr the session does not satisfy and the person could reach, prompt=select_account, or an id_token_hint naming another person (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1). A login made during the interaction answers all of them, the hint excepted, which only a session of the person it names answers. With prompt=none, a request that needs a login is answered login_required instead (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6). Authorization requests say how each is read.
  • A page of the account that adds or takes away a way in, when the newest proof of the session is more than five minutes old. The account pages list them.

docs.title: The snapshot a grant reads
docs.text: When an authorization is granted, the session is read once: its auth_time, its amr, and the acr answered to the request, which is the class the request asked for that the session satisfies, or the class the session answers with when the request asked for none. Those three values are frozen into the grant, and every token that descends from it carries them, the code, the refresh token, the access token and the ID token alike. A later login on the same session moves the session, and never a token already issued.

docs.title: Ending one
docs.text:
What ends it Ended by The end session endpoint, OIDC RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 relying_party A LogoutRequest of a SAML service provider relying_party Close, on the page of the sessions of the account user Close every other one, on the same page, which keeps the session reading it user A password replaced on the page of the account, which ends every other session of the person user beffroi:user:revoke-session, with the identifier beffroi:user:sessions lists user A login of another person on the same browser user

The first end wins, and a session that has ended authenticates nothing afterwards. The act session.ended goes to the journal of the person.

Every end revokes what was issued under it. On the lane of the events, beside the back-channel logout that tells the clients of the session (logout), its refresh tokens are revoked, rotated ones included, and its opaque access tokens removed, the revocation dated by the end of the session and not by the moment the lane reached it. The provider refuses every token of an ended session at its use, in the meantime and afterwards: UserInfo and introspection refuse an access token whose session ended, and the token endpoint a refresh token whose session ended, revoking again what a refresh in flight had saved. A resource server that verifies a self-contained access token offline accepts it until it expires, ten minutes by default (beffroi.tokens.access_token_ttl).

Expiry is not an end

A session past its twelve hours signs nobody in and is not offered to the browser that held it, and no option changes that duration. Nothing is announced when it passes, though, and nothing is revoked: the refresh tokens and access tokens issued under it keep the lifetimes they were issued with. What has not been exchanged yet, an authorization code, a device code or a backchannel request, is refused at the token endpoint once its session has expired.

The row of a session, ended or not, is dropped by an hourly step once its expiry is older than the absolute lifetime of a refresh token family plus the lifetime of an access token, ninety days and ten minutes with the defaults: until then, a token issued under it can still be presented, and its session is what answers for it.

docs.title: The events of the core
docs.text: The core dispatches PSR-14 events and nothing else: it knows no bus and no broker. An event is built where it is raised, its constructor takes exactly what it carries, and it carries a domain object only when that object survives the queue it may be written to, the facts by identifier otherwise. The protocol and the SAML package raise events of the same shape, and the reference lists every one of the three packages with what listens to it.

docs.title: What every event carries
docs.text:
Every event implements DomainEventInterface, and so carries four things:

Member What it is name() The name of the act, which the journal writes down: a label the event gives itself, such as user.authenticated, and never a class name occurredAt When it happened tenant The tenant it happened in context The provenance of the request it came from: when the request was received, the address and the user agent. A command of the console names itself, the user of the shell and the host in place of a user agent, beffroi-console/<command> (<user>@<host>), and a timed step names the schedule and the host, beffroi-scheduler/beffroi (<host>), both with no address

Two interfaces say more of an event that means more:

Interface What it adds Read by ConcernsAPersonInterface subject(), the person the act concerns, by the subject their account carries and never by the sub a client was given, a pairwise one included. Null where the act named nobody: a login refused on an identifier no account answers happened to no one this provider knows The journal, which files the act under that person SessionProvenanceInterface sessionId(), the session whose row holds the very provenance the event carries The enrichment that finds the place of that provenance and writes it on the row of the session

An event that names a domain object carries it whole, as its row holds it: a credential with its hash or its envelope and the person it belongs to, a session with its two provenances, a key with its sealed private half. That is why the body of every message is sealed on its way out. What reaches the journal of the acts is the act, its date, its provenance, sealed, the subject and the client, and nothing else of what the event carries. An event that names facts carries the facts and no more: person.provisioned carries the subject and the name of the provider, never what the provider said, and an archive is named by its identifier and never carried.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
Act Class Raised when Carries beyond the four user.authenticated UserAuthenticated A session is opened, whatever proved it The session, whose opening gives the event its date and its provenance authentication.failed AuthenticationFailed A login is refused, whatever was tried The method the attempt claimed, null when a passkey ceremony failed before naming one; the reason; the identifier as typed, null when nothing was typed; the user, null when no account answers session.ended AuthenticationSessionEnded A session ends, whatever ended it The session, which says who ended it: user or relying_party, the two the bundle writes password.used PasswordUsed A password is accepted, whether or not a code follows The credential passkey.used PasskeyUsed A passkey assertion is verified The credential, and whether its sign count did not grow totp.used TotpUsed A code of the authenticator application is accepted The credential backup_code.used BackupCodeUsed A backup code is spent The credential person.provisioned PersonProvisioned An upstream provider creates a person, at their first sign-in through it The subject of the person and the name of the provider

The reason of a refused login is one of unknown_user, no_such_credential, invalid_credential, disabled_user, revoked_credential, replayed_code, too_many_attempts, expired_login, below_the_floor, federated_domain, upstream_response_refused and upstream_person_refused. It is written for the audit, and the person is told no more than the page needs: the login page says the same thing whatever the reason, and the page of a code says apart when too many codes have been tried.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: Act Class Raised when Carries beyond the four credential.enrolled CredentialEnrolled A passkey or a TOTP is enrolled The credential credential.renamed CredentialRenamed A person renames a passkey The credential, and the name it had credential.revoked CredentialRevoked A credential is revoked The credential credential.forgotten CredentialForgotten The floor of the tenant forgets a credential, row and secret The credential, the only trace left of it password.changed PasswordChanged A person replaces their own password The credential password.rehashed PasswordRehashed A password is stored again under the current algorithm and parameters The credential backup_codes.renewed BackupCodesRenewed A person draws another set of backup codes The credential, and never a code enrolment_ticket.issued EnrolmentTicketIssued An administrator issues an enrolment ticket The ticket, which holds a hash of its value

docs.title: The person and their record
docs.text: Act Class Raised when Carries beyond the four person.described_themselves PersonDescribedThemselves A person says something of themselves on their account The user, the name of the claim, and whether they took it back archive.asked PersonAskedForTheirArchive A person asks for their archive The identifier of the archive and the subject of the person archive.taken PersonTookTheirArchive A person downloads their archive The same archive.dropped PersonDroppedTheirArchive A person has their archive dropped The same

docs.title: Keys and data keys
docs.text: Act Class Raised when Carries beyond the four tenant.key_staged TenantKeyStaged A key is drawn and staged, used for nothing yet, and published in the JWK Set when its algorithm is one the set carries The key tenant.key_rotated TenantKeyRotated A key takes over The key activated, and the key it replaced, null for the first of its algorithm tenant.key_retired TenantKeyRetired A key leaves the service The key, and why: due, forced or compromised tenant.data_keys_rewrapped TenantDataKeysRewrapped The data keys of the tenant are wrapped by another client How many keys over how many scopes, the client they came from when one was named, the client and the master key that wrap them from then on tenant.data_keys_destroyed TenantDataKeysDestroyed The data keys of the tenant are erased How many keys over how many scopes

docs.title: The deployment
docs.text:
Act Class Raised when Carries beyond the four kms.unavailable KmsUnavailable The key management service of the tenant does not answer, or refuses, on the path of a request What the service said, and never a secret, a key or an envelope load.budget_spent LoadBudgetSpent A request is refused because a budget that bounds a load is spent The budget, the route asked for, and the client the budget was counted on, null for the budget of an origin

The page of the account that reads the journal of a person shows every act of this list that concerns a person, password.rehashed excepted, which is this provider storing a hash again and nothing the person did.

docs.title: How they leave
docs.text:
In the bundle, the dispatcher the core is handed is EventBusDispatcher, which replays every event on the event.bus of Messenger; an event raised by the handler of a message leaves once that handler has committed its work. Every event is routed by the interface they all implement to the transport async_priority_low, the database unless the deployment names a broker, and its body is sealed to the message key of the tenant on its way out. Nothing listens in the process that raised it: a worker that consumes the transport is where every listener runs, and an event nothing listens to is announced all the same.

What listens is a message handler of event.bus. The handlers of the bundle are classes marked #[AsMessageHandler(bus: 'event.bus')] whose __invoke() is typed on an event, or on an interface every event of a kind implements, which is how the one that writes the journal hears every event of the three packages. Messenger describes the buses and the transports.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: A group belongs to a tenant and holds members, and every membership carries its source: written here, asserted by an upstream identity provider, or pushed by a directory. That is what lets a provider accept memberships from outside without a directory silently taking over what somebody decided here, and what tells a person reading their own file which door to knock on.

docs.title: What a group is
docs.text:
Field What it holds Name Unique within the tenant and compared exactly, case included. In Unicode Normalization Form C, without whitespace at either end, 255 characters at most Source Where the group comes from: local for every group, a group being created here and never by a provider Created at When it was created

A membership is a group, a person of the same tenant, the source of that membership and the date it was added. The table holds one membership per group and person, whatever its source.

docs.title: Where a membership comes from
docs.text: Source What it is What writes it local A membership decided in this provider No command or page of the bundle writes one upstream_claims A membership an upstream identity provider asserted at the last sign-in The sign-in through that provider, when its declaration maps groups scim A membership a directory pushed Nothing: SCIM is not implemented

docs.title: A group is created here
docs.text:
The group itself is local. An operator creates it, and its name is taken as it is typed, never trimmed or folded, since the declaration of a provider names it exactly:

bin/console beffroi:group:create Staff

A name the rules above refuse is refused, and so is a name the tenant already holds. The command prints the name, the source, the identifier of the row and the slug of the tenant.

No provider creates one. The declaration of an upstream identity provider maps the values of an attribute to the names of groups of the tenant. A value the map does not name, a name the tenant holds no group under, and a value that is not a string are ignored: what a provider sends never becomes a group.

docs.title: What a provider asserts
docs.text:
The memberships a provider asserts are what it said at the last sign-in. At each sign-in of a person that provider created, when its declaration maps groups:

  • a membership of source upstream_claims whose group it no longer asserts goes;
  • one whose group it still asserts stays, with the date it was added;
  • a group newly asserted gets one, of source upstream_claims.

The removals are written before the additions, in the same unit as the rest of the sign-in, so all of it is kept or none of it, and before the session the sign-in opens serves anything: nothing that session serves reads a membership the provider has taken away.

A membership of another source is left as it is. A membership of source local or scim stays when the provider asserts its group, which gives no second membership, and stays when the provider stops asserting it. A provider whose declaration maps no groups leaves every membership as it was, and a person an operator linked by hand to a provider, which did not create them, is given none.

docs.title: Reading them
docs.text:
beffroi:user:show lists the groups of a person, each with the source of the membership and the date it was added, and the archive a person asks for carries the same three facts in its groups chapter.

No claim of OpenID Connect and no SAML attribute carries the groups of a person to a client.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text: title: Keys description: The keys of a tenant: what each one is for, sealed by the key management service, published or kept, and rotated without an outage.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
A tenant signs and decrypts with keys it owns, each one sealed by a key management service: the private half is sealed before anything is written, and the master key that seals it never leaves the service. A key has an algorithm, which says what it is for, a status and the dates of its life, and the JWK Set publishes the ones a client may need, a key staged for a rotation and a key still retiring among them.

A rotation is therefore not an outage: the new key is published before it is used, and the old one stays published until nothing it signed can still arrive.

docs.title: What a key is for
docs.text:
The algorithm of a key is what it is for, and the use its JWK publishes (RFC 7517 §4.2) is checked against the algorithm rather than trusted: a key that signs never opens anything, and a key that is encrypted to never signs. A tenant holds one active key per algorithm.

Algorithm Use Published What it is RS256 sig In the JWK Set The default signature algorithm, the first wired: what signs a self-contained access token and a signed introspection response, and the ID token or the signed authorization response of a client that registered no algorithm for it, a logout token following the ID token. RSA, 3072 bits PS256 sig In the JWK Set RSA, 3072 bits ES256 sig In the JWK Set P-256 EdDSA sig In the JWK Set Ed25519 ECDH-ES+A256KW enc In the JWK Set What a client encrypts to the provider with, over P-256 RSA-OAEP-256 enc In the JWK Set The same, RSA, 3072 bits MESSAGE-SEAL enc Kept What the body of every message written to a transport is sealed to, as a JWE under ECDH-ES+A256KW and A256GCM VAPID sig Kept The key a browser is handed when it subscribes to web push (RFC 8292), wired where web push is turned on SAML-SIGNING sig Kept The SAML key of the tenant, which both SAML roles sign with and whose certificate their metadata carry, wired where a SAML role is turned on SAML-ENCRYPTION: and an entity ID enc Kept The key one upstream SAML identity provider encrypts for, one per provider declared

An RSA key is drawn at 3072 bits, 2048 being the floor the code refuses to go under. A kept key is a key of the tenant like the others, with the same custody, the same statuses and the same commands, and none of them appears in the JWK Set: a key the JWK Set published would be one any reader of it could encrypt to or verify against. The key of a capability a deployment turns off stays where it is, served, rotated and drawn by nothing, and is back in service as it was the day the capability is turned on again.

The message key is the first key of a tenant. A body is sealed to it or not written at all, and every other key announces its own staging on a transport, so a tenant is given that one before any other:

bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=MESSAGE-SEAL
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate

The second line draws a key of the default signature algorithm. --algorithm names any other, among those the deployment is wired with.

docs.title: Custody
docs.text:
The private half of a key is drawn in the process, sealed in an envelope by the key management service the configuration names, and only then written; the master key never leaves that service, and the private key never reaches it. The envelope is bound to the tenant, and told from the envelope of a TOTP secret: sealed for one tenant, it does not open for another. The kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the public key, SHA-256, so the same material carries the same name whoever drew it, and one material is the key of one algorithm: a second algorithm under a kid already held is refused.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    keys:
        kms: op
        key_id: '%env(BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID)%'
Option Default What it decides kms required The key management client that seals the keys, an entry of key_management.clients key_id required The master key of that service the keys are sealed under, {tenant} standing for the slug of the tenant, one master key each storage %kernel.project_dir%/var/keys The directory of the sealed keys, one JSON file per key under the slug of its tenant, written through a sibling file renamed into place jwks_max_age 300 How long a client may cache the JWK Set, in seconds, which the staging delay derives from staging_delay jwks_max_age plus sixty seconds How long a new key is published before it is used, in seconds age 7776000, ninety days How long a key works before a successor is staged behind it, in seconds, counted from its activation

Key management says how the clients are declared. A process opens a key once and keeps it open for as long as it is the key that answers, so a worker that serves many requests asks the service once per key, where a process rebuilt at each request asks at each request. A key another has replaced, or that has retired, is let go.

docs.title: The life of a key
docs.text:
Status Published What it does What moves it on staged Yes Signs nothing yet; a JWE a client encrypted to it opens Its staging delay elapsing, or beffroi:keys:activate active Yes The one key of its algorithm in use: the key that signs, for a key of the sig use A successor taking over retiring Yes Signs nothing; what it signed still verifies, and what was encrypted to it still opens Its retirement date passing, or beffroi:keys:retire retired No Nothing: a JWS naming its kid is refused, a JWE encrypted to it does not open Nothing, retired is the last status

"Published" is said of the algorithms the JWK Set carries; a kept key goes through the same four statuses without ever being published. The key a body is sealed to is the newest MESSAGE-SEAL key in service, a staged one included, since nobody reads the JWK Set for it.

A retiring key stays for its window. When a key takes over, the one it replaces starts retiring until the longest lifetime among what is bound to a key of its use has passed. For a key of the sig use, that is the ID token, the self-contained access token where a client of the tenant is registered for that shape, the logout token while its delivery may still be tried where back-channel logout is served, and the signed authorization response where a response mode that signs is served. For a key of the enc use, that is the longest a request object is accepted to stand and the lifetime of a pushed authorization request. beffroi:keys:list shows the date each retiring key is due.

docs.title: Rotating without an outage
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:keys:rotate

beffroi:keys:rotate draws a new key of its algorithm, the default signature algorithm unless --algorithm names another, and publishes it at once. The key in use stays the active one until the staging delay has elapsed, and a client that cached the JWK Set has seen the new key before anything is signed with it. Then the new key takes over, and the old one retires with its window.

Option What it changes None The new key is staged and takes over once its staging delay has elapsed --now The new key takes over at once. A relying party whose copy of the JWK Set is younger than sixty seconds refuses the new tokens, or encrypts to the old key, until its copy is that old --compromised The new key takes over at once, and the active one leaves the JWK Set in the same call, with no window: nothing it signed is honoured afterwards

A tenant that holds no active key of the algorithm gets the new key active at once, whatever the options, since nobody caches an empty JWK Set. beffroi:keys:generate is beffroi:keys:rotate --now under another name, for the first key of a tenant.

Command What it does beffroi:keys:activate <kid> A staged key takes over before its delay has elapsed; the active one starts retiring beffroi:keys:retire <kid> A retiring key leaves the JWK Set, once its retirement date has passed beffroi:keys:retire <kid> --force The same before its date, for a key nothing bound to can arrive any more, or after a compromise beffroi:keys:retire --due Every retiring key past its date, which is what the timed step does

The active key is never retired by hand: a tenant without an active key signs nothing, so a rotation comes first. Each step writes its act to the journal, tenant.key_staged, tenant.key_rotated and tenant.key_retired, and the event of a retirement carries why: due when its date had passed, forced when it had not, compromised after --compromised.

docs.title: What time does on its own
docs.text:
A timed step runs every minute, on the scheduler_beffroi transport the worker consumes, and does three things in an order that lets one tick finish what the previous one began:

  1. A key that has worked for its age gets a successor, staged and not activated, when nothing of its algorithm is staged already. Nobody has to ask, and a deployment nobody watches does not sign with the same key for ever.
  2. A staged key whose delay has elapsed takes over, and the key it replaces starts retiring.
  3. A retiring key past its date leaves the JWK Set.

The age has to be longer than the retirement window of the use of the key, or every rotation would leave one more key in the JWK Set: the step refuses an age that is not, the first time a key reaches it, rather than staging a successor.

beffroi:keys:list --check opens the active and the staged keys with the key management service, says of an active key whether it has worked past its age and whether a successor is staged behind it, and fails on a key that does not open, or on an active key past its age with nothing staged: from outside, that is what a schedule that has stopped looks like. --all lists the retired keys too.

docs.title: The figures of a family
docs.text:
How long a new key is staged and how long it works is the schedule its family declares, so a key that costs somebody a step at every rotation is not rotated at the pace of one nobody sees:

Family Staged for Works for Set by The keys of the JWK Set, and MESSAGE-SEAL and VAPID beside them the max-age of the JWK Set plus sixty seconds, 360 seconds by default ninety days beffroi.keys.staging_delay, beffroi.keys.age SAML-SIGNING, and the SAML-ENCRYPTION key of each upstream identity provider seven days 365 days beffroi.saml.identity_provider.staging_delay, age

The SAML keys are staged for a week because their next certificate is published in metadata that service providers fetch once a day, and that some administrators upload by hand. The identity provider says why each figure is what it is.

docs.title: When the service loses a key
docs.text: A key management service that does not answer, or refuses, makes the request that needed a key answer 503 with a Retry-After of ten seconds, and the act kms.unavailable is written: nothing was refused to anybody, and the same request is served once the service is back. A service that lost its master key leaves envelopes nothing opens. beffroi:keys:list --check names each active or staged key it cannot open, with its algorithm. For a dead active key, the way out is a rotation per algorithm, beffroi:keys:rotate --now --algorithm=<name>: the new key is sealed under the master key the service holds and takes over at once, and the dead key retires with its window, its public half still verifying what it signed. Nothing is deleted. A rotation leaves a dead staged key where it is, and the timed step activates it once its delay has elapsed, as it activates any staged key.

docs.title: Linked identities
docs.text: A linked identity says that a user of this tenant is a given subject at a named upstream provider. Whoever presents that subject at that provider is that user, and nobody else: it is what keeps a person from being created again every time they arrive by another door, and the one way a subject an upstream provider names becomes a person of this tenant at all. Nothing infers one. A row is written by a sign-in through the provider, or by an operator, and by nothing else.

docs.title: What one holds
docs.text:
Field What it holds Provider The upstream provider, named as the federation knows it: the entity ID of an upstream SAML identity provider, or the identity_provider of a trusted issuer Subject The value that provider gives the person, compared byte for byte. It is not the sub this provider issues Claims The last snapshot of what the provider said of the person, empty when it said nothing Linked at, last seen at When the link was written, and when it was last written again

The pair names one person of the tenant. The store holds one row per provider and subject, and linking a pair to a second person is refused, naming the person it already names. Linking it again to the same person is what a second run of an import does: the snapshot is replaced and the date it was last seen moves, the row keeps its person.

It is sealed. The provider, the subject and the snapshot are personal data, sealed under the data key of the tenant like every column of a person.
