        kms: op
        key_id: '%env(BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID)%'
        storage: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/keys'
    clients: []

A name key_management.clients does not hold fails the build of the container. The firewall of the pages, the session cookie and the rest an application writes are on installing the bundle.

The issuer is the exact string the provider announces as iss and the prefix every endpoint is served under. It is not a cosmetic setting: a client compares it byte by byte, and it never changes for a tenant. Every token the tenant issued names it, so a configuration that names another issuer for the same tenant is refused rather than served: another issuer is another tenant, under another slug.

The whole configuration tree

docs.title: As an application of its own
docs.text:
If you have no application to host it, do not write one. beffroi/op is the Symfony skeleton, the bundle and FrankenPHP already assembled, and it is the deployment the project supports.

The standalone application

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. The tenant and its keys, without which nothing can be signed.
  2. Your first client, so something can ask for a token.
  3. A Symfony relying party, to see a sign-in end to end.

docs.title: The tenant and its keys
docs.text: A provider that cannot sign cannot answer. Two things happen before the first request: the tenant of the configuration gets its row, and it gets a key.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
The bundle ships its Doctrine migrations, and registers their path with doctrine/doctrine-migrations-bundle when the application has it, which provides the command:

bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate

docs.title: The tenant
docs.text:
The tenant is declared in the configuration, not created by a command: the issuer is a property of the deployment. The command writes the row that matches what the configuration says.

bin/console beffroi:tenant:synchronize

It writes what the configuration says of the tenant, its name, its look, the claims its people may change of themselves and the classes it answers with, and prints the tenant it synchronised. Run it on every deployment. The issuer is the one thing it never changes: every token a tenant issued names it, so a configuration that gives a tenant another issuer is refused, by this command and by the provider, which serves nothing while its row and its configuration disagree. Another issuer is another tenant, under another slug.

docs.title: Its first keys
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=MESSAGE-SEAL
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate
bin/console beffroi:keys:list

The key the messages are sealed to comes first. Nothing the provider writes to a transport leaves the process in clear, and drawing any other key announces its own staging on a transport: on a tenant that does not hold a MESSAGE-SEAL key yet, that announcement has nothing to be sealed to, and the command fails. Then comes the signing key of the default algorithm, and then a key for each further algorithm the deployment serves, SAML-SIGNING among them for a tenant that speaks SAML.

beffroi:keys:generate draws a key, seals it with the configured key management service and makes it the active key of its algorithm at once. That is the right command for an empty deployment and the wrong one for a live deployment, where beffroi:keys:rotate replaces a key without an outage: it stages the new key, publishes it in the JWK Set immediately, and lets it take over once the staging delay has elapsed, so a client that cached the key set still verifies what it receives.

Check that the keys in use can actually be opened:

bin/console beffroi:keys:list --check

That opens the keys in use, and the ones about to be, with the key management service, and fails on one it cannot open or one that has worked past its age with nothing staged behind it. It is worth running in a deployment pipeline: a key the provider cannot open is an outage at the first token request, not at the next rotation.

A key works for an age, ninety days unless the configuration says otherwise, counted from the moment it became active, and a year for the SAML signing key, whose family has figures of its own. Reaching it is not an outage either: a timed step stages a successor without anybody asking for one. That is what --check reports of an active key, in one of three answers: it has not worked past its age, it has and a successor is staged behind it, or it has and nothing is staged. The last one fails the run, because a planning that has stopped looks exactly like that from outside.

docs.title: A user
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --email alice@example.com
bin/console beffroi:user:set-password alice

The subject the clients will know Alice by is generated and stable. You pass --subject only when you are importing an identity that already has one somewhere else.

Keys, in full

docs.title: The standalone application
docs.text: title: The standalone application description: beffroi/op on your machine and as a deployment of its own: the development stack, the production image, and the first start in the order it has to happen.

docs.title: The standalone application
docs.text:
beffroi/op is a provider you deploy rather than a provider you assemble: a Symfony skeleton on the bundle, served by FrankenPHP in worker mode, with PostgreSQL for the model and RabbitMQ for the writes the protocol does not wait on. It is the deployment the project supports, and the development stack the conformance plans run against is this application.

It is the apps/op directory of the monorepo, beffroi-auth/beffroi. Its composer.json resolves the beffroi/* packages through path repositories to ../../src/*, so the application is built from a working copy of the monorepo: beffroi-auth/op is a read-only mirror of that one directory, and installs nothing on its own.

docs.title: What it adds to the bundle
docs.text:
The bundle brings, with the packages under it, the protocols, the identity model, the pages and the commands. The application brings what a deployment decides, and nothing else.

What Where it lives The layout of the pages and their stylesheet, Tailwind and DaisyUI, built by the standalone Tailwind binary it pins templates/, assets/styles/app.css The theme a visitor reads the pages in, light, dark or the one of their system, chosen by a form posted to /theme src/Theme/ Its own page of what the provider holds of a person, at /account/profile, which says under the field that was refused why it was src/Controller/, src/Form/ The root of the issuer, /, which sends a browser to the home of the account config/routes/home.yaml The firewall of the interaction pages, with the four logins of the bundle: a password, a passkey, a code, and an upstream SAML identity provider config/packages/security.yaml The headers a deployment answers with, and the name and attributes of the session cookie config/packages/nelmio_security.yaml, nelmio_cors.yaml, framework.yaml The transports of Messenger, on RabbitMQ config/packages/messenger.yaml FrankenPHP and Caddy, with the host that asks for a client certificate frankenphp/ One type of authorization detail, invoice_payment (RFC 9396 §2), the bundle wiring none src/AuthorizationDetails/

docs.title: On your machine
docs.text:
The development stack runs the application in Docker beside PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. It is driven from the root of the monorepo by Castor, 0.23 or later, and asks the machine for Docker Compose and Composer besides. The two composer install below run on the machine and not in a container, so it also needs PHP 8.4 or later with the extensions the locked packages require, intl, dom, zip and amqp among them.

git clone git@github.com:beffroi-auth/beffroi.git && cd beffroi
composer install && (cd apps/op && composer install)
castor start
castor provision

castor start brings up the provider on https://op.localhost, the host that asks for a client certificate on https://mtls.op.localhost, PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. On a machine with an mkcert authority, the stack serves a certificate mkcert issues there for its names, which a browser that trusts mkcert accepts; on any other, Caddy issues one from its internal authority. On a stack that names no key management service yet, the worker is created and left stopped, because it refuses to start without one.

castor provision is what a first start needs, in order, and it can be run again at will:

  1. it writes into apps/op/.env.local what is missing there: the key management service, a sodium key generated in place unless --kms file, --kms vault or --kms aws names another backend, the secrets of the clients the stack declares, and the password of the development user;
  2. it plays the migrations;
  3. it writes the row of the tenant with beffroi:tenant:synchronize;
  4. it draws the keys of the tenant, the key messages are sealed to first, or checks with the key management service that the keys already there still open;
  5. it creates the user alice with a verified email address, describes her with the claims of the profile, phone and address scopes, and sets her password;
  6. it issues the client certificate of the stack, on the machine, under var/mtls/;
  7. it starts the worker.

It ends by printing where the discovery document and the JWK Set are, the key management service, the username, password and subject of alice, and the secrets of the clients. https://op.localhost/ sends a browser to the home of the account, which asks it to sign in.

The clients of the stack are declared for the development environment only: the clients of the OpenID conformance suite, and those of the demonstrations of the repository, among them oidc-demo. castor stop takes the stack down, castor logs follows its logs and castor console runs a console command in the container that serves it.

docs.title: As a deployment of its own
docs.text:
The production image is built from the root of the monorepo, which is the build context its Dockerfile expects:

docker build --file apps/op/Dockerfile --target frankenphp_prod .

The build copies apps/op/ of the working copy as it stands, installs the application without its development dependencies, compiles .env for production with composer dump-env prod, builds the stylesheet and compiles the assets. composer dump-env compiles a .env.local too when one is there, and the one the development stack writes holds its key management service, the secrets of its clients and the password of its user: the image is built from a checkout that holds no .env.local. What changes from one machine to the next is then read from the environment when the container starts: the issuer, the database, the broker, the key management service.

The environment the application reads

docs.title: The first start, in order
docs.text:
The order is the one of castor provision, and two of its constraints hold for every deployment: the tenant has a row before it has a key, and its first key is the one messages are sealed to.

  1. The schema. The container that serves HTTP waits for the database and plays the migrations before FrankenPHP starts, every time it starts.

  2. The tenant and its keys, in a container of the image:

    bin/console beffroi:tenant:synchronize
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=MESSAGE-SEAL
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate

    Drawing a key announces it on a transport, and what goes on a transport is sealed to the key the tenant keeps for its messages. That key is therefore the first one: a tenant that does not hold it yet has beffroi:keys:generate fail on the message it cannot seal. The second command draws the key of the default signature algorithm, RS256, which the access tokens are signed with, and the ID tokens of a client that names no other algorithm.

  3. The keys of what this application turns on. Its configuration turns on web push and the SAML identity provider, each with a key of its own:

    bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=VAPID
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING

    The discovery document announces every algorithm the bundle is wired with, and a key is drawn for each one a client uses: a client that registers ES256 for what the provider signs for it needs the key of ES256, and one that encrypts to the provider with ECDH-ES+A256KW the key of that algorithm. The development stack draws both.

  4. A person who can sign in:

    bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --email alice@example.com
bin/console beffroi:user:set-password alice

  5. The worker, once the steps above are done: the same image, running bin/console messenger:consume on the schedule and the four lanes of the provider.

The image, the processes and the worker

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. The tenant and its keys, for what each of those commands does.
  2. Your first client: outside development the application declares none.
  3. A Symfony relying party, to see a sign-in end to end.

docs.title: Your first client
docs.text: A client is an application the provider answers. It has an identifier, a way of authenticating itself, and the exact addresses it may be sent back to.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Clients a deployment knows in advance are declared in the configuration. The key is the client_id.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        my-application:
            client_name: 'My application'
            secret: '%env(MY_APPLICATION_SECRET)%'
            redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/oidc/callback']
            post_logout_redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
            scope: 'openid profile email offline_access'
Field What it means client_name What a person reads on the consent page. It is the name of a stranger until you set it secret Never written in the file. An environment variable, and only for a confidential client redirect_uris The addresses the browser may be sent back to, compared exactly. One entry per address, no pattern post_logout_redirect_uris Where the browser may be sent after a logout, compared the same way token_endpoint_auth_method The one method this client authenticates with. A client authenticates with the method it registered and no other, RFC 6749 §2.3.1 scope The ceiling of what this client may ask for. Asking for more is refused, asking for less is normal

docs.title: A public client
docs.text:
A client that cannot keep a secret does not get one: no secret, and token_endpoint_auth_method: none. PKCE is what protects it, and a public client cannot be exempted from it.

beffroi:
    clients:
        my-desktop-application:
            client_name: 'My desktop application'
            redirect_uris: ['http://127.0.0.1/oidc/callback']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: none
            scope: 'openid profile offline_access'

A native application receives its code on the loopback interface, named by its IP literal, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], and never by a name (RFC 8252 §8.3), on whatever port it opened: for a public client, a loopback redirect URI is the one comparison that ignores the port (RFC 8252 §7.3). A custom URI scheme is refused (RFC 8252 §7.1), so a mobile application registers an https URI it claims (RFC 8252 §7.2).

docs.title: What the provider refuses
docs.text:
• A redirect URI that is not in the list, even by one character, even by a trailing slash. The one difference accepted is the port of a loopback URI registered by a public client, above.
  • An authorization request with code_challenge_method=plain, always, and one without code_challenge, unless the client is a confidential one registered with requires_pkce: false. A public client cannot be.
  • A client authenticating with a method other than the one it registered.
  • A scope the client was not granted.

docs.title: Reading what exists
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:client:list
bin/console beffroi:client:show my-application

The listing covers every client of the tenant, the ones the configuration declared and the ones that registered themselves, each saying which it is. A client that registered itself can be deleted with beffroi:client:delete; one the configuration declares cannot, because the configuration would put it back.

Clients, in full and client authentication

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
This section holds one page per version that asks something of you, with the changes listed and the way to make them.

There is nothing here yet: no version of Beffroi is released, so no version has to be migrated from. The first page will appear with the first release that changes a public interface.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• Until 1.0, a minor version may change the public API. What changes is listed here, with the reason and the replacement, before the version is published.
  • A migration page describes the version it belongs to, read from the version selector at the top of the page. It never describes a version you are not reading.
  • A database change ships as a Doctrine migration, never as a sentence telling you to run some SQL.
  • A removal is announced before it happens. A deprecation in one minor version, the removal in the next major one.

docs.title: Coming from another provider
docs.text:
Three things exist, and one does not.

  • The subjects can be kept. beffroi:user:create --subject creates a person under the sub the clients already know them by, so an application that stored it finds the same person.
  • The old provider can stay where it is, upstream. An identity provider that speaks SAML 2.0 is declared upstream of the tenant: the people of its domains sign in there, and each is created here at their first sign-in, with the claims and the groups its declaration maps.
  • A person who exists here can be tied to it by hand, with beffroi:user:link, and then signs in under that link.
  • A password hash cannot be imported. No command takes one: a password is set from its value, and a person without one poses a passkey from an enrolment ticket or signs in through their organisation. Importing the people of a directory as they are is what SCIM will serve.

docs.title: Index
docs.text: title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect description: What beffroi/oidc implements: clients, authorization requests, grants, tokens, discovery, logout.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
docs.text: beffroi/oidc is the protocol, in pure PHP, on top of the identity core. It knows no HTTP: it reads values, applies the rules of the specifications, and returns what the answer must contain. Turning that into a request and a response is the job of the bundle.

docs.title: The shape of a sign-in
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Beffroi
    C->>P: Authorization request (PAR, or in the URL)
    P->>B: Login page, then consent
    B->>P: Credentials, then the answer
    P->>C: Redirect with the code, and iss
    C->>P: Token request, with the PKCE verifier
    P->>C: Access token, ID token, refresh token
    C->>P: UserInfo, with the access token

Every step of that exchange has a page below, and each page cites the section of the specification it describes.

docs.title: What is served
docs.text:
• Clients

    What a client is, where it came from, what it registered, and how it authenticates.

  • Authorization requests

    What is read, what is refused, PKCE, and the iss that goes back in every response.

  • Grants

    Authorization code, refresh token, client credentials, device code, CIBA, token exchange, JWT bearer.

  • Tokens

    Access tokens as at+jwt or as references, ID tokens, refresh tokens, and what is encrypted.

  • Discovery and JWKS

    The document the provider publishes, derived from what is wired rather than from a list kept beside it.

  • Logout

    RP-initiated, front-channel and back-channel, and what each one can promise.

docs.title: Hardening a client can ask for
docs.text: The provider does not need a different deployment to serve a demanding client. The same endpoints accept pushed authorization requests, signed request objects, signed and encrypted responses, and tokens bound to a key with DPoP or to a certificate with mutual TLS. A client that asks for none of it keeps working, and the FAPI 2.0 profiles are what prove the strict end of that range.

docs.title: One source of truth
docs.text: What the provider announces is derived from what it is wired with. The discovery document reads the grants that are tagged, the client authentication methods that are registered and the algorithms that are available, so there is no list to keep in agreement with the code. Enabling a grant announces it; removing it stops announcing it. Discovery and JWKS says what that produces.

docs.title: Authorization details
docs.text:
authorization_details is how a client asks for an authorization a scope cannot describe: an amount, an account, a document, a named action. The provider validates each detail against the types it supports, shows the person what is being asked, and puts what was granted in the token.

This page will describe the types, the validation, and what the consent page shows of them.

docs.title: Authorization request
docs.text:
The authorization endpoint reads the request, finds the client, compares the redirect URI exactly, requires PKCE with S256, and decides whether a person has to be shown a page at all. Every response carries iss (RFC 9207), so a client can tell which provider answered it.

This page will describe each parameter, the order the checks run in, and which errors go back to the client rather than to the person.

docs.title: Client authentication
docs.text:
A client authenticates with the one method it registered and no other (RFC 6749 §2.3.1): a secret sent as HTTP Basic or in the body, a JWT it signed with its own key (private_key_jwt, RFC 7523), a mutual TLS certificate (RFC 8705), or nothing at all for a public client. A method is a class implementing the interface of that capability, and what the provider announces is what is wired.

This page will describe each method, what it requires of a client, and what the provider checks.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
A client is an application the provider answers, identified by a client_id, holding the redirect URIs it may be sent back to, the methods it authenticates with and the metadata it registered. A client declared by the configuration and a client that registered itself are the same object with a different source, and the source is visible wherever clients are read.

This page will describe the model, every piece of metadata a client may hold, and what the provider refuses at registration time rather than at request time.

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
Consent is recorded, scoped to a client and a person, and it extends itself rather than being rewritten when a client asks for more. A person reads what they agreed to and takes it back from their account pages, and a command does the same thing for an operator.

This page will describe the model, when a person is asked again, and what revoking consent takes away.

docs.title: Discovery and JWKS
docs.text:
/.well-known/openid-configuration (OIDC Discovery 1.0) and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server (RFC 8414) describe the provider, and /jwks publishes the keys a client needs to verify what it receives. Both documents are derived from what is wired: a grant, a client authentication method or an algorithm appears there because it exists, never because somebody added a line.

This page will describe every field published, what is cacheable, and what changes during a key rotation.

docs.title: Dynamic registration
docs.text:
Registration is served when the tenant says so, and the tenant decides the mode: who may register, what an initial access token buys, and whether an authority it pinned may vouch for a piece of software this provider never issued. A registered client then reads, replaces and deletes itself at the URI it was handed (RFC 7592).

This page will describe the modes, the initial access tokens, the software statements, and what is refused.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An error is either redirectable, in which case it goes to the client at a redirect URI that was validated first, or it is not, in which case the person sees a page and the client learns nothing. Confusing the two is how an open redirector is born.

This page will list the error codes, say which are redirectable, and describe what is recorded about each.

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text:
An interaction is the part a person sees: signing in, proving a second factor, agreeing to what a client asks. The request waits on it, identified rather than held in a session, so a person can finish it in another tab and so a provider restricted to the protocol plane never serves it.

On a tenant that federates domains, the login of an interaction asks for the address first, and an address of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for is sent to that provider; a login_hint that is such an address sends the browser there without showing the page. What the client asked of the login, prompt=login, a max_age or a step-up, is asked of the provider in turn and checked against the instant the person authenticated there: signing in through an organisation says how.

This page will describe the model, prompt, max_age, acr_values, and what a client learns of an interaction that did not finish.

docs.title: Introspection and revocation
docs.text:
Introspection describes a token to the client it was issued to and to nobody else, as JSON or as a signed JWT. Revocation ends a token and what depends on it, and it answers the same way whether the token existed or not.

The signed form is RFC 9701: the response is a JWT, application/token-introspection+jwt, for a client that registered that it wants one, and the algorithms it may be signed with are announced in the discovery document beside the endpoint itself.

An answer that hands a person over is an act of their journal. An introspection that describes an active token issued for a person tells a third party who that token names, so it is written, introspection.answered, naming the client that asked and the person. An answer active: false writes nothing, and neither does the description of a token a client holds for itself, which hands over nobody.

This page will describe both endpoints, who may call them, what introspection returns, and what a revocation reaches.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
Three specifications, and they are not interchangeable: RP-initiated logout is a client asking for a session to end, front-channel logout tells the other clients through the browser, and back-channel logout tells them server to server with a signed logout token. A provider that implements only the first one has not logged anybody out of anywhere else.

A session is shared with SAML. The session a client signed in under is the one the SAML service providers of the browser signed in under too. When it ends at the end session endpoint, the front-channel logout page comes first, and the browser then goes on to tell each SAML service provider of the session before it reaches the post_logout_redirect_uri: single logout says how that chain is played.

Every end of a session revokes what was issued under it. At the end session endpoint, from the page of the account, by the console, by a SAML logout request or replaced by a new login: the refresh tokens issued in the session are revoked and its opaque access tokens removed, beside the back-channel logout tokens sent to its clients, and the provider refuses every token of that session from then on. A resource server that verifies a self-contained access token offline accepts it until it expires.

This page will describe each one, what a client registers for it, and what a logout can and cannot promise.

docs.title: Pairwise subjects
docs.text:
With a pairwise subject identifier, two clients in different sectors see two different sub for the same person, and cannot correlate their users by comparing them. The sector is what the client declares, and the identifier is stable for that sector.

This page will describe the calculation, the sector identifier, and what a client must do about it.

docs.title: The ports of the protocol
docs.text:
The protocol package needs repositories for its clients, its codes and its tokens, a reader for a client's key set, a source of randomness and a clock. Each port is small and per capability, and a use case sees only what it calls.

This page will list the ports and what ships in the bridge.

docs.title: Pushed authorization requests
docs.text:
The client pushes its authorization request to the provider, authenticating itself, and receives a request_uri the browser then carries. Nothing of the request travels in a URL, and the provider knows the request was not tampered with on the way.

This page will describe the endpoint, the lifetime of a request_uri, and what a tenant may require.

docs.title: Request objects
docs.text:
A request object is the authorization request as a JWT the client signed, so the provider reads what the client meant rather than what a browser passed along. A client registers the algorithm it will sign with, and one that registered nothing is never read an unsigned object.

This page will describe the object, the algorithms, request against request_uri, and the rules about what may differ between the object and the query.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
A client names the resource it intends to call, and the token is issued for that audience rather than for everything the client might reach. A resource server that receives a token addressed elsewhere refuses it.

What a tenant announces as its protected resources is read from the clients that registered one, never from a list kept beside them, and it is the protected_resources member of RFC 9728 §4: the one member of the registry that says what the values of a resource parameter are, RFC 8707 registering none of its own. A tenant whose clients registered none announces nothing rather than an empty list, which a client would read as "no resource is acceptable here".

This page will describe the parameter, what the issued token carries, and what happens when several resources are named.

docs.title: Response modes
docs.text: title: Response modes status: draft description: How the answer travels back: query, form post, or a signed JWT.

docs.title: Response modes
docs.text:
The response mode decides how the authorization response reaches the client: in the query, in a self-submitting form (form_post), or as a signed and optionally encrypted JWT (JARM). A signed response is what lets a client prove the answer came from this provider and was not rewritten.

This page will describe each mode, what a cross-site POST does to a session cookie, and what JARM carries.

docs.title: Scopes and claims
docs.text:
A scope is a request for claims, and claims asks for them one by one (OIDC Core §5.5). The provider gives what the person agreed to, what the client is allowed, and what it actually holds, which is the intersection and never the union.

This page will describe the standard scopes, the claims parameter, and where a claim is read from.

docs.title: UserInfo
docs.text:
UserInfo answers the claims the access token allows, for the person it was issued for, as JSON or as a signed and optionally encrypted JWT. It is the one endpoint where the answer depends on the token and on the consent behind it rather than on the request.

Every answer is an act of the journal of that person, userinfo.answered, naming the client it was given to: it is one of the two reads that hand a personal datum to a third party. It is written once the answer exists, so a request that could not be answered is no line of it.

This page will describe the request, the claims returned, and the signed and encrypted responses.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
A grant is a class implementing the grant interface, tagged in the wiring; the token endpoint holds no match on a grant type, and the discovery document announces exactly the grants that are tagged. What a grant can do is declared by the interfaces it implements: whether it sends a person to the client, whether it issues refresh tokens, whether it acts for the client itself, whether it exchanges a token.

Grant type Page authorization_code Authorization code refresh_token Refresh token client_credentials Client credentials urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code Device code urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba Backchannel authentication urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange Token exchange urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer JWT bearer

The resource owner password credentials grant is not in that list and never will be.

docs.title: Authorization code
docs.text:
A code is single use, short lived, bound to the client it was issued to, to the redirect URI it was asked for and to the PKCE verifier that will be presented. Spending it yields the tokens the request asked for and nothing more.

This page will describe the exchange, every check it runs, and what a replayed code does.

docs.title: Backchannel authentication
docs.text: title: Backchannel authentication status: draft description: CIBA: the device that asks is not the one that answers.

docs.title: Backchannel authentication
docs.text:
In CIBA (CIBA Core 1.0) the client asks the provider to reach a person it names, and the person answers on their own device. The client then polls, or is pinged, and the two FAPI-CIBA profiles are what judge this implementation.

This page will describe the request, the hints that name a person, the poll and ping modes, and how the person is actually reached.

docs.title: Client credentials
docs.text:
There is no person in this grant: a confidential client asks for a token for itself, for the resource it named. No ID token is issued, no consent is involved, and no refresh token is given, because the client can simply ask again.

This page will describe what the token carries, and what a resource server reads of it.

docs.title: Device code
docs.text:
The device asks for a code, shows it to the person, and polls while they confirm it in a browser somewhere else. The provider answers authorization_pending and slow_down as the specification requires, and the confirmation page is part of the interaction plane.

This page will describe both endpoints, the polling rules, and the lifetime of a device code.

docs.title: JWT bearer
docs.text:
A client presents a JWT signed by an issuer the tenant has pinned, and gets a token in exchange. What the tenant trusts is declared explicitly: an issuer, its keys, and what it is allowed to assert.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    trusted_issuers:
        'https://issuer.example.com':
            jwks_uri: 'https://issuer.example.com/jwks.json'
            signing_algorithms: ['ES256']
            clients: ['gateway']
            identity_provider: example-issuer
            trusted_scopes: ['invoices.read']
Option What it decides The key The iss the issuer signs with. An issuer nobody declared is unknown jwks or jwks_uri Its keys, inline or read back from a URL, one or the other and never both. A URL is read with one GET over HTTPS, no redirect followed, kept in a pool the workers share, and read again at most once per cooldown when an assertion names a kid the kept set does not hold, which is how an issuer that rotates its keys is followed. The keys are the only ones an assertion is verified against, whatever its header names (RFC 8725 §3.10) signing_algorithms The algorithms an assertion may be signed with, among those the provider is wired with clients The clients that may present its assertions. An issuer trusted for a gateway is not trusted for every client identity_provider The source of the linked identities its subjects name: a sub is a person of the tenant only when a linked identity of that source says so, and nobody is ever created from an assertion trusted_scopes What it is trusted for. openid buys nothing here, the grant authenticating nobody

A link between a person and a subject of the issuer is written by an operator, with beffroi:user:link and the name given in identity_provider.

This page will describe what is checked of an assertion, and what it may obtain.

docs.title: Refresh token
docs.text:
A refresh token renews an access token without the person being there, which is why it is the one the rules are strictest about: it has a lifetime and an absolute lifetime, it keeps the authentication snapshot of the session that created it, and spending it may replace it.

This page will describe rotation, reuse detection, what a revocation takes with it, and what offline_access changes.

docs.title: Token exchange
docs.text:
Token exchange is how a gateway acts on behalf of a service, or a service on behalf of a person, without either of them handing over their own token. The result names the subject and the actor, and a resource server can tell them apart.

The issued token knows the person it is about. Its sub is the one the presented token carried, written for the client that token was issued to (RFC 8693 §2.2.1), which may be a pairwise subject the client that asked cannot read. So the provider keeps the person beside it: on the record of an opaque token, and, in a self-contained one, as a private claim person sealed by the key management service of the tenant, which the provider alone can open and which tells the holder nothing it did not know. That is what lets introspection describe an exchanged token, and the act that describes it lands in the journal of that person. A token a client holds for itself is about nobody, and carries no such claim.

This page will describe the parameters, delegation against impersonation, and what the issued token claims.

docs.title: Sender-constrained tokens
docs.text:
A bearer token is worth whatever stealing it is worth. A sender-constrained token is bound to something the client proves it holds on every call: a key with DPoP, or a client certificate with mutual TLS. The binding is carried in the token's confirmation claim, and a resource server checks it.

A confirmation method is a class implementing the interface of that capability, which is why both methods work on both shapes of access token.

docs.title: DPoP
docs.text:
The client signs a proof with a key it holds, the provider binds the token to the thumbprint of that key, and a resource server refuses the token to anybody who cannot sign a matching proof. It works for a public client, which is what makes it the useful one for a mobile or browser application.

This page will describe the proof, the nonce, the replay window, and what a resource server must check.

docs.title: Mutual TLS
docs.text:
A client authenticates with a certificate, and the token it receives is bound to that certificate's thumbprint. The provider reads the certificate the TLS listener actually validated, from the edge to PHP, and refuses one carried in a header by whoever felt like adding it.

This page will describe both halves of RFC 8705, the endpoint aliases a provider announces for them, and how the certificate reaches the application.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
Three kinds of token leave this provider, and a client never has to guess which it is holding: an access token for a resource server, an ID token about the person, and a refresh token to ask again. Encryption says what the provider encrypts and for whom.

A token format is a class implementing the issuer interface of that format, so adding one is adding a class and announcing it follows from wiring it.

docs.title: Access tokens
docs.text:
An access token here is at+jwt (RFC 9068) or an opaque reference, per client, and never an ambiguous shape: a resource server must know what it is validating. Both carry the same facts, and both can be bound to a key or a certificate.

This page will describe the claims of an at+jwt, what introspection returns for a reference, and how the format of a client is chosen.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
A client may register that it wants its ID token, its UserInfo response or its authorization response encrypted, with the algorithms it supports and the key it publishes. The provider then encrypts for that client and for nobody else, and announces only what it can actually do.

This page will describe the registration, the algorithms, where the keys come from, and what fails when a key set cannot be read.

docs.title: ID tokens
docs.text:
An ID token is a statement about an authentication, addressed to one client: who the person is, when they proved it, how, and with which provider. It is signed, it may be encrypted, and it is never a credential for an API.

This page will describe the claims, what nonce, auth_time, acr and amr carry, and the algorithms a client may register.

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text:
A refresh token is the longest lived thing the provider issues, so it is the one with the most rules: a lifetime and an absolute lifetime, the authentication snapshot of the session it came from, and a chain that a reuse breaks.

This page will describe storage, rotation, reuse, and what revoking one takes with it.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
The exhaustive tree, option by option, with the type, the default and what it decides. It is generated from the configuration classes of the bundle, so it cannot drift from what the container validates.

Until it is generated into this page, bin/console config:dump-reference beffroi prints the same thing from your own installation, including the sections your version actually has.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
Every command of the bundle is prefixed beffroi:, and those that act on identity act on the tenant the configuration names. A command that reads is never the command that writes: beffroi:user:show reads, beffroi:user:profile writes, and they are two classes.

Run bin/console beffroi:<group>:<command> --help for the arguments and the options of one of them; the table below is the map.

docs.title: The deployment and the tenant
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:doctor Say whether this deployment holds together: one line per point looked at, and what to do about the ones it does not answer for. Reads and writes nothing, so it is safe on a provider serving traffic, and it fails when a point is red so a deployment pipeline can ask the question too. beffroi:tenant:login-floor Name the floor of every login of the tenant, and forget the credentials it forbids. beffroi:tenant:synchronize Write the row of the tenant of the configuration: created, renamed, or left alone.

What beffroi:doctor looks at is what is wired, one class per point, so a deployment that adds a point adds a class. It looks at every one of them before it answers: a doctor that stops on the first thing that is broken never reaches the second.

beffroi:tenant:login-floor takes the name of a predicate, single_factor, two_factors, phishing_resistant or phishing_resistant_hardware, and writes it on the row of the tenant rather than in a file, since hardening a tenant is an act with a date. It asks before it runs, because every credential the floor reads nothing of is forgotten, its secret and its row: under phishing_resistant, the passwords, the one-time codes and the backup codes of every person go. Lowering the floor afterwards gives nobody back what was forgotten. The floor of its logins says what it changes.

docs.title: Users, their credentials and what they agreed to
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:user:applications List the applications a user agreed to, with what each one holds of them and what it has asked that is still waiting. beffroi:user:create Create a user of the tenant; give them a password with beffroi:user:set-password. beffroi:user:enrolment-ticket Issue the link that lets a person pose their first passkey, and print it. beffroi:user:journal List the acts of a user over a period, with the application each one was done on behalf of; for answering a request about what happened in their name. beffroi:user:link Say that a user of the tenant is a given subject at an upstream provider; run again to refresh it. beffroi:user:profile Describe a user with the standard claims of OIDC Core section 5.1; what is not said is cleared, except what the upstream provider that created the user holds, which is kept, and saying that otherwise is refused; a run that says nothing writes nothing. To read a user, see beffroi:user:show. beffroi:user:reindex Derive again the blind indexes of every person of the tenant, after the projection of one changed. beffroi:user:revoke-consent Take back the consent a user gave a client, and the access it holds; the next authorization request asks again. beffroi:user:revoke-credential Revoke a credential of a user by its identifier; the credential stays listed as revoked. beffroi:user:revoke-session End a session of a user by its identifier; the relying parties of that session are told by the back-channel. beffroi:user:sessions List the sessions open in the name of a user, with what each one proved and where it was last seen. beffroi:user:set-password Set or replace the password of a user, asked on the terminal or read from the standard input. beffroi:user:show Show a user: the identity with the source that created it, the standard claims that are set, the credentials with their kind, identifier, name and dates, and the groups with the source of each membership.

An enrolment ticket is for a person who has nothing to sign in with yet, on a tenant that signs its people in by passkey and holds no password of theirs to give them. The link opens one enrolment of a passkey, once, for seventy-two hours, and it is printed once: the row holds a hash of what it carries. Issuing another one for the same person takes the first one away, and a disabled account gets none. It proves no login either: the session that follows comes from the passkey that was just posed.

The journal of a person is read over --from and --to, two days in UTC, both included, narrowed with --act, repeatable, and --client, and written as a table or, with --format=json, as the document a request under article 15 of the GDPR is answered with. A period that reaches past what the deployment keeps is answered with how long it keeps an act and the day that reaches, never with an empty table that looks complete.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:group:create Create a group of the tenant, which the declaration of an upstream provider may map the groups it asserts to.

No upstream provider creates a group: the declaration of one maps the values it asserts to groups that exist already, by their name, and a value naming a group the tenant does not hold is no group.

docs.title: Clients and initial access tokens
docs.text: Command What it does beffroi:client:delete Delete a client that registered itself; a client declared in the configuration is refused. beffroi:client:list List the clients of the tenant: where each came from, when it was registered and when it was last used. beffroi:client:show Show a client of the tenant: where it came from, its dates, and what it registered. beffroi:client:token:issue Issue an initial access token for the tenant; the value is printed once and never again. beffroi:client:token:list List the initial access tokens of the tenant: what each has served, what it has left and whether it still authorises anything. beffroi:client:token:revoke Revoke an initial access token by its identifier; it authorises no registration from that instant.

docs.title: Signing keys
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:keys:activate Make a staged key the active one of its algorithm before its staging delay elapsed; the key it takes over from starts retiring. beffroi:keys:generate Generate a key, seal it with the configured KMS and make it the active one of its algorithm at once; "beffroi:keys:rotate" is the rotation without an outage. beffroi:keys:list List the keys of the tenant with their use, status and dates: the published ones, or every key with --all; --check opens the keys in use, or about to be, with the KMS and fails on one it cannot open, or that has worked past its age with nothing staged behind it. beffroi:keys:retire Take a retiring key out of the JWK Set: one key by its identifier, before its retirement date with --force; or every key past its date with --due. beffroi:keys:rotate Stage a new key, sealed by the configured KMS and published at once; it takes over once the staging delay elapsed, or at once with --now; --compromised retires the previous key with no window.

--algorithm names the key a command acts on: a JWS algorithm for a key that signs tokens, a JWE key management algorithm for a key clients encrypt to, or one of the keys the tenant keeps rather than publishing, among them SAML-SIGNING, the key both SAML roles sign with, and SAML-ENCRYPTION: followed by the entity ID of an upstream identity provider, the key that provider encrypts for. Left out, it is the default signature algorithm.

docs.title: Data keys
docs.text: Command What it does beffroi:data-keys:destroy Erase the data keys of the tenant, which makes every personal datum it had sealed unreadable for good. Asks for the slug to be typed back. Cannot be undone. beffroi:data-keys:list List the data keys of the tenant by scope, with when each was minted, the master key that wraps it and the KMS client that opens it; reads only, and never opens a key. beffroi:data-keys:rewrap Wrap the data keys of the tenant with another KMS client from now on, or with another master key of the same one; --dry-run lists what would move. No sealed value is read or rewritten.

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:geoip:refresh Download the GeoLite2 databases of addresses now, refuse what is not one, and store them for the enrichment of a provenance; --url for a mirror or a file already unpacked.

A timed step runs the same object once a week, which is the cadence the databases are published at, so the command is for installing them the day a deployment subscribes and for reading why a refresh was refused. A deployment that names no licence key downloads nothing and serves every flow with a provenance that says an address and no place.

docs.title: SAML metadata
docs.text:
Command What it does beffroi:saml:service-provider:refresh Read the metadata of the service providers the configuration declares, or of one of them, and keep each document accepted; an expired or an older document is refused and the one accepted kept. beffroi:saml:service-provider:forget Forget the metadata accepted for a service provider, so that the next refresh registers it again as a first one; the refresh refuses older documents only against what is accepted. beffroi:saml:identity-provider:refresh Read the metadata of the upstream identity providers the configuration declares, or of one of them, and keep each document accepted; an expired or an older document is refused and the one accepted kept. beffroi:saml:identity-provider:forget Forget the metadata accepted for an upstream identity provider, so that the next refresh registers it again as a first one; the refresh refuses older documents only against what is accepted.

A timed step runs the same refresh every hour for the peers of both roles, so the command is for the first reading of a peer just declared and for reading why a document was refused. Forgetting is never a step of the schedule: it is the one way back from a signed document an operator decides to stop holding the provider to.

SAML 2.0

docs.title: Passkeys and FIDO metadata
docs.text: Command What it does beffroi:webauthn:mds-import Store a metadata statement file (unsigned, trusted as the file is) next to the FIDO Metadata BLOB, for the keys of a manufacturer the service does not list or the authenticators of the FIDO conformance tools. beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh Download the FIDO Metadata BLOB, verify its signature under the pinned root and store it for the passkey ceremonies; --url for another service, --root for another root.

docs.title: What a command may not do
docs.text: A command never bypasses a rule the protocol applies. It cannot mint a token for a user, cannot read a signing key it is not allowed to open, and cannot read a personal datum the key management service refuses to unseal. beffroi:data-keys:destroy is the one that cannot be undone, and it asks for the slug of the tenant to be typed back before it runs.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Paths are relative to the issuer, which is where the application imports the routes of the bundle. A deployment whose issuer is https://op.example.com serves the token endpoint at https://op.example.com/token.

Every route name carries its plane. beffroi_protocol_* is server to server, called by a client or a resource server; beffroi_interaction_* is a browser, where a person reads a page and answers. The BEFFROI_PLANE environment variable restricts a process to one plane, so an interaction never reaches a machine that only serves the protocol, and the other way round.

docs.title: The protocol plane
docs.text:
Method Path Route Specification GET /.well-known/openid-configuration beffroi_protocol_discovery OIDC Discovery 1.0 §4 GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server beffroi_protocol_authorization_server_metadata RFC 8414 GET /jwks beffroi_protocol_jwks RFC 7517 POST /token beffroi_protocol_token RFC 6749 §3.2 GET POST /userinfo beffroi_protocol_userinfo OIDC Core §5.3 POST /introspect beffroi_protocol_introspection RFC 7662, RFC 9701 POST /revoke beffroi_protocol_revocation RFC 7009 POST /par beffroi_protocol_pushed_authorization_request RFC 9126 POST /device_authorization beffroi_protocol_device_authorization RFC 8628 §3.1 POST /backchannel_authentication beffroi_protocol_backchannel_authentication CIBA Core §7 POST /register beffroi_protocol_client_registration RFC 7591 GET /register/{client_id} beffroi_protocol_client_configuration_read RFC 7592 §2.1 PUT /register/{client_id} beffroi_protocol_client_configuration_update RFC 7592 §2.2 DELETE /register/{client_id} beffroi_protocol_client_configuration_delete RFC 7592 §2.3

The endpoints a deployment actually announces are the ones it has wired. The discovery document is built from what is wired, never from a list kept beside it, so a grant you did not enable is not advertised.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The core, beffroi/oidc and beffroi/saml dispatch PSR-14 events, and the bundle replays them on Messenger. Every event names its act, the date it happened, its tenant and the provenance of the request it came from, as the events of the core describe; the tables below say what each one carries beyond those four, and who it concerns:

  • a person, when it implements ConcernsAPersonInterface and names the subject of their account, never the sub a client was given;
  • a client, when it implements ConcernsAClientInterface and names the client by the identifier it was registered under, never the client itself.

docs.title: Every event crosses the broker
docs.text: An event is routed to the transport async_priority_low, the database unless the deployment names a broker, every one of them by the interface they all implement, so an event added to a package leaves the process without a line of configuration. Its body is a JWE to the message key of the tenant; what stays readable on the transport is the class of the event, its stamps and the slug of its tenant. Nothing listens in the process that raised it, and an event nothing listens to is announced all the same.

docs.title: What listens
docs.text:
Every event is written to the journal. WriteTheActDownHandler hears every event of the three packages and writes one row: the act, the date, the provenance, sealed, the subject when the event concerns a person and the client when it concerns a client, and nothing else. A row is kept beffroi.journal.retention days, 180 by default, and beffroi:user:journal reads it back for a person.

The other listeners of the bundle each hear one event, or an interface a few of them implement:

Listener Hears What it does BackChannelLogoutHandler session.ended Mints a logout token for each client of the session that registered a back-channel logout URI (Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.6), each one raising logout_token.issued RevokeTheTokensOfTheSessionHandler session.ended Revokes the refresh tokens of the session and removes its opaque access tokens, dated by the end of the session RevokeWhatOutlivedTheSessionHandler refresh_token.outlived_its_session The same again, dated by the end of the session, for what a refresh in flight had saved EnrichTheProvenanceHandler user.authenticated, through SessionProvenanceInterface Finds the place of the two provenances of the session and writes it on its row BuildThePersonalArchiveHandler archive.asked Builds the archive the person asked for RecordClientUseHandler authorization_code.issued and tokens.issued, through ClientInUseInterface Dates the last use of the client, which the removal of the clients nobody uses reads WriteWhatTheClientWasGivenHandler tokens.issued Writes, beside the act, what the client was given of the person, kept as long as the act QueueLogoutTokenHandler logout_token.issued Hands the token to the notifications lane, async_notifications, which posts it to the client QueueClientNotificationHandler backchannel_request.answered Hands the call to the notification endpoint of the client to the same lane RecordTheServiceProviderOfTheSessionHandler saml.service_provider.signed_in Records the part of the service provider in the session, for the logout the identity provider starts

A logout token its client refuses is given up at once. One that cannot be delivered is tried again on the schedule of beffroi.back_channel_logout, and goes to the failure transport once that schedule runs out. Either way, logout_token.given_up is raised.

docs.title: SAML 2.0
docs.text: SAML 2.0 is still what a large part of the installed base speaks, and an identity provider that cannot answer it cannot replace the one a company already has. Beffroi serves it in both roles, on the tenant, the people and the sessions OpenID Connect uses: one person of the core, two protocols to reach them. A browser signed in by one is signed in for the other, and a session that ends ends for both.

Both roles are off by default, and each is a switch of its own. A deployment that turns neither on draws no SAML key and publishes no metadata, and every message that reaches its single sign-on or single logout service is refused, nobody being declared to send one: nothing of this section costs anything to a provider that does not use it.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        identity_provider: true
        service_provider: true

The peers themselves, the service providers on one side and the upstream identity providers on the other, are declared in the same section, keyed by their entity ID. They are configuration and nothing else: no request registers one and no page edits one.

docs.title: What is served
docs.text:
Paths are relative to the issuer, as every route of the bundle.

Method Path Role What it is GET /saml/metadata identity provider The metadata of the identity provider. Its URL is its entity ID GET POST /saml/sso identity provider Single sign-on, over HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST at the one URL GET POST /saml/slo identity provider Single logout, over both bindings, a request or an answer GET /saml/sp/metadata service provider The metadata of the service provider. Its URL is its entity ID unless the deployment names another GET /saml/sp/metadata/{identity provider} service provider The same metadata with the encryption certificates meant for one upstream identity provider POST /saml/sp/acs service provider The assertion consumer service, over HTTP-POST

A role the deployment did not turn on serves nothing. The metadata of that role answer 404, and so do the sign-on and the assertion consumer service of the service provider; the single sign-on and single logout services of the identity provider refuse every message, as one of an issuer nobody declared. The endpoints lists the routes behind them, the ones a login sends a browser back through included.

docs.title: What is always true
docs.text:
None of the rules below has an option. They are properties of the code, held by its tests, and a peer that needs one of them relaxed is a peer this provider does not serve.

Rule Why Every assertion the identity provider writes is signed, and every response over it, under RSA-SHA256. Every assertion the service provider takes is covered by a signature, its own or its response's A service provider that verifies either finds a signature, an assertion stands alone as the statement of the tenant, and nothing unsigned is read as a statement of anybody SHA-1, MD5, HMAC, DSA and ECDSA are refused, in an XML signature and over the query string of HTTP-Redirect A verifier that honours the algorithm a message names verifies what the attacker made verifiable An assertion sent encrypted is encrypted under AES-256-GCM, its key under RSA-OAEP. Nothing is ever encrypted in CBC CBC authenticates nothing, which is what padding oracles are made of A message is read only in what a signature covers Signature wrapping hands the verifier one element and the reader another A peer's keys come from its metadata, never from the KeyInfo of a message A message that names the key it is verified with verifies under the attacker's key Every assertion and every logout message is accepted once A message taken off the wire is not a second login, nor a second logout A peer is declared by the deployment, and its metadata come from a file of the deployment or an https URL, no redirect followed A peer registered by a request, or metadata fetched wherever a redirect points, is a peer an attacker chose Every endpoint a browser is sent to is https on a host An assertion posted in clear, or to a javascript: URL, is an assertion given away A response nobody asked for is refused, and no assertion is sent unasked Nothing binds an unsolicited response to the browser that carries it, which is how a victim is signed in to an attacker's account

The XML underneath goes through one hardened loader, which refuses a document type declaration, an entity, two elements under the same identifier and a document past its bounds before anything reads it, and a SAML message, a metadata document or a signature is never parsed any other way. The SAML packages says what each of the libraries guarantees.

docs.title: What is not served
docs.text:
• The Artifact and SOAP bindings, SAML 1.x and WS-Federation. A single logout reaches a service provider through the browser that ended the session, never server to server.
  • Metadata aggregates of an inter-institution federation: an md:EntitiesDescriptor is refused by name, and each peer is declared on its own.
  • An administration interface for the peers. They are configuration, and the console reads and refreshes their metadata.
  • Single logout with an upstream identity provider, which the metadata of the service provider do not announce.
  • Sign-on started by an identity provider. Every assertion the identity provider writes answers an AuthnRequest, and every response the service provider takes answers a request it sent.
  • The groups an upstream identity provider asserts are memberships of the tenant. No claim hands them to a client of OpenID Connect.

docs.title: Signing in through an organisation
docs.text:
Once a tenant declares an upstream identity provider, the people of its domains sign in there and nowhere else. The person who arrives at the login page is sent to the identity provider of their organisation, signs in as they do every morning, and comes back to the client or to the page that was waiting, as a person of the tenant.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant P as Beffroi
    participant I as Identity provider of the organisation
    B->>P: The login page asks for the address
    B->>P: alice@example.org
    P->>B: A signed AuthnRequest, to the provider of example.org
    B->>I: The person signs in there
    I->>B: A signed Response
    B->>P: POST /saml/sp/acs
    P->>B: The interaction goes on, a code goes to the client

docs.title: The login page asks for the address first
docs.text:
When the tenant has an upstream identity provider, the login page of an interaction shows one field, the address, and nothing else: no password, no passkey, no passkey offered by the browser's autofill. The same holds for the login a page of the provider asks for on its own, the approval of a device, a request waiting for an answer, the pages of the account or the single sign-on of a service provider. A tenant without an upstream identity provider shows the usual page.

The field is posted to /login/address, and what was typed decides where the browser goes:

What was typed Where the browser goes An address of a domain an identity provider answers for To the sign-on of that identity provider, /saml/sp/sign-on, by a 303, which sends it on to the provider An address of any other domain Back to the usual login page, its username field holding what was typed, with a way back to the address A value without an @ The same: a username, of no domain An address whose domain cannot be read Back to the page of the address, which says so

The domain is read one way everywhere it is read: the whole part after the last @, through the IDNA of UTS #46 into its A-label, lower-cased, so an address typed in capitals, in Unicode or in its A-label belongs to the same domain.

Nothing here reads a person. The answer depends on the domain and on the declarations of the tenant, and on nothing else: the page answers the same status, the same headers and the same body whether somebody holds that address or not, and waits on no lookup a clock could tell apart. The field holds what this browser typed last, or the login_hint of the request when it is an address, as the client wrote it.

A login_hint of a federated domain skips the page. When the authorization request carries a login_hint (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1) that is an address of a domain an identity provider answers for, the login page sends the browser to that provider at once and shows nothing. Every later render of that login goes there again: such an interaction is signed in through the identity provider or not at all.

docs.title: The request sent upstream
docs.text:
The sign-on starts at /saml/sp/sign-on, and only from the login page: the redirection that sends the browser there carries a reference drawn for that login and kept in the session of that browser, used once and valid one minute. A sign-on that presents no reference, or one this browser was not given, writes no request: a page of another site can send a browser to that route but cannot read its session, so nobody can start the login of a person who did not ask for one and have it answered by a session held elsewhere.

The request is an AuthnRequest written and signed by the SAML key of the tenant:

What Value Where it goes The first single sign-on service of the accepted metadata on HTTP-Redirect, or on HTTP-POST when the provider offers no other, never an address a request or a page names Signature RSA-SHA256, over the query string for HTTP-Redirect, in the XML for HTTP-POST Issuer The entity ID of the service provider of the tenant AssertionConsumerServiceURL /saml/sp/acs, with the HTTP-POST binding NameIDPolicy persistent, with AllowCreate="true" ForceAuthn When the client asked for a login the session of this browser cannot answer, and when a page asks a signed-in person for a fresh proof RelayState 32 random bytes in base64url, and nothing else: no URL, no value of the request

ForceAuthn follows what the login page itself would ask of a browser that holds a session of the provider: prompt=login, a max_age that session exceeds, a step-up, prompt=select_account, an id_token_hint naming another person. A browser that holds no session forces a login for prompt=login alone, and the age of what the person proved is checked when the response comes back. Without it, a session the person left open at their identity provider would answer a client that asked for a fresh login.

The request is remembered in the HTTP session of the browser, under its RelayState, for ten minutes, eight at most per browser: what a response answers is read there, and nowhere else.

The address can go with it. An identity provider that reads a hint on its sign-in page is declared with address_parameter, login_hint for Microsoft Entra ID, and the address typed on the login page, or the login_hint that skipped it, is added in that parameter: after the Signature over HTTP-Redirect, outside what is signed, and in the query of the form's action over HTTP-POST. It goes only to the provider that answers for its domain, and it is a hint and never a proof: the person is who the signed assertion names, whatever the form at the provider was prefilled with.

docs.title: The response taken back
docs.text:
The assertion consumer service is /saml/sp/acs, POST only, a body in application/x-www-form-urlencoded and nothing else (415). The identity provider posts it from its own site, so it arrives without the session cookie, and it is posted again once from the provider's own origin, as a sign-on request is.

A response nobody asked for is refused. The RelayState has to name a request this browser remembers, sent less than ten minutes ago, and it is forgotten as it is read, so a form posted twice finds nothing the second time. A response that answers no request this provider sent cannot be told apart from one an attacker obtained for their own account, which is how a victim gets signed in to the attacker's.

It is verified under the provider the request went to, never under one the message names: its InResponseTo is that request, its Issuer that provider, its Destination and Recipient the URL of the assertion consumer service, its Audience the entity ID of the service provider. Every assertion is covered by a signature, its own or the response's, made by a key of the provider's metadata, and is accepted once. An encrypted assertion is opened by the keys of that provider alone.

A response whose status is not Success carries no assertion and signs nobody in. The person cancelled or failed at their identity provider, so the client is answered access_denied at its redirection URI with its state, or login_required when the provider answered NoPassive to a request with prompt=none (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6), and nothing the identity provider wrote reaches the client.

Every refusal is a page that names the rule and never a value of the response, opens no session and writes nothing of the person. A response the service provider does not take, a person it may not sign in and a login under the floor of the tenant are each written to the journal as a refused login, with the method fed.

docs.title: The person
docs.text:
Named by the provider, never by an address. The subject is the value of a persistent NameID, or, for a provider declared with subject_attribute, the one value of that attribute. A subject that is the same mailbox as the address of the assertion is refused whatever names it, so a mailbox given to somebody new never leads to the account of the one who held it.

Found by the link, never by the address. The person is the one whose linked identity names that provider and that subject. At the first sign-in there is none, and the person is created in one unit, all of it kept or none of it:

  • the person, its subject drawn as any other, its username its address, the address verified, the provider answering for its domain;
  • its source, the identity provider, with the claims of the profile it filled;
  • its linked identity, with what the provider said;
  • a telephone number, unverified, when the profile maps one;
  • its memberships, the groups the declaration maps the values of the groups attribute to.

The address has to be in a domain of that provider, and held by no other person of the tenant, as a mailbox or as a username: an existing account is never linked on its own. An administrator who wants a person who already exists to sign in through a provider links them by hand, naming the entity ID of the provider and the subject it gives that person:

bin/console beffroi:user:link alice 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata' 'the-subject-it-gives-alice'

A person linked that way signs in under the link with none of the rules of a first sign-in, only the snapshot of the linked identity being refreshed.

The provider keeps what it fills. At every later sign-in, what the source holds becomes exactly what the provider fills and says now, the memberships it asserts are replaced, and the username follows the address when the provider sends another one. A claim it no longer says is released to the person, with the value it wrote last. What the source holds, neither the person on the page of their account nor an operator with beffroi:user:profile can change.

A disabled person is refused before anything of them is written: an account an administrator disabled keeps what it held and stops following the provider. The page says what it says of every refusal, and nothing of the state of the account.

docs.title: The session
docs.text:
What Value amr fed, a federated assertion, and the class of the provider where its meaning is exactly a method (RFC 8176 §2): Password and PasswordProtectedTransport add pwd, Smartcard adds sc, TimeSyncToken adds otp, any other class adds nothing auth_time The AuthnInstant of the assertion, the instant the person authenticated at their provider, never the instant the response arrived Its end No later than the SessionNotOnOrAfter the provider set, which is the one way it has of ending the session it vouches for. An assertion whose SessionNotOnOrAfter has passed is refused

The session is opened under the floor of the tenant, like every login: a tenant that asks for two factors refuses a login that proved fed and pwd alone.

What the client asked is held at the response. A login made during the interaction, an AuthnInstant at or after the instant it began, satisfies prompt=login, a max_age and a step-up. An earlier one does not: the request is sent once more with ForceAuthn when the first one did not carry it, and when it did, the client is answered login_required, or account_selection_required for prompt=select_account. A request is never sent a third time, so a provider that ignores ForceAuthn never sends the browser round without end. The comparison has no tolerance for clocks, and a provider whose clock lags by more than the time a person takes to sign in answers login_required until its clock is set.

The browser goes back to what was waiting, and nowhere a response or a parameter names: the login page of the interaction, which resumes it and sends the code to the redirection URI the client registered, or the page of the provider that asked for the login.

docs.title: No local credential for an organisation's people
docs.text:
A person whose address is of a domain an identity provider answers for, their mailbox or a username holding an @, signs in through that provider and through nothing else.

  • At the login, a password, a passkey and the code that completes a password are refused for them, whatever the page offered, so a form written by hand fails as the page would. A refused password answers as a wrong one, at the cost of a wrong one, and the journal records why.
  • On the pages of the account, no form that would pose a password, a passkey or an authenticator application is offered, and the page says why: their organisation signs them in.
  • Anywhere a credential is posed, the console setting a password, an enrolment ticket for a passkey, a TOTP, a renewal of backup codes, the replacement of a password held before the domain was federated: the answer is the same refusal.

So a person who leaves the organisation and loses their account in its directory has no local password left that outlives the departure.

On a tenant with an upstream identity provider, an address whose domain cannot be read counts as one of a federated domain, refused rather than taken for an address of none. The account an administrator keeps for the day the identity provider is down therefore has a username without an @, or an address in a domain of two labels at least that no provider declares, and never one such as admin@localhost.

docs.title: The identity provider
docs.text: The tenant is the SAML identity provider of the service providers it declares: they send it an AuthnRequest, and it answers with a signed assertion about the person signed in. This page is the role itself, its key and the document that describes it. Service providers is how one is declared, and single sign-on what a request gets.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        identity_provider:
            enabled: true
Option Default What it decides enabled false Whether the role exists at all. Off, its metadata answer 404, no service provider may be declared, and every message at its single sign-on and single logout services is refused want_authn_requests_signed true What the metadata say in WantAuthnRequestsSigned (SAML Metadata §2.4.3) staging_delay 604800, seven days How long a new SAML signing key is published in the metadata before it signs, in seconds age 31536000, 365 days How long a SAML signing key works before a successor is staged behind it, in seconds, counted from its activation cache_duration 86400, one day The cacheDuration of the metadata (SAML Metadata §2.3.2), in seconds: how long a service provider keeps them before it fetches them again. One second at least, and strictly shorter than staging_delay, which the configuration refuses otherwise

The three figures belong to the deployment and not to a tenant, as those of beffroi.keys do, and they are the figures of the SAML key whichever role draws it: the service provider of the tenant signs with the same key.

want_authn_requests_signed is an announcement, and nothing more. It tells a service provider configured from the metadata to sign its requests, which is what a broker such as SimpleSAMLphp does when it reads true. Whether a request that arrives needs a signature is decided per service provider, by its declaration and its own metadata, and the setting neither adds a signature to that rule nor takes one from it: the signature a request needs says how.

docs.title: The key
docs.text:
The SAML signing key is a key of the tenant like every other one. Its algorithm is SAML-SIGNING, an RSA key of 3072 bits, the size every RSA key of the tenant is drawn at. The key pair is drawn in the process, its private half sealed by the key management service before anything is written, and opened in memory when the process signs. It is not in the JWK Set and it is not in the metadata: what the metadata publish is a certificate around its public half.

Turning a role on does not draw a key. On a deployment that has none, draw it once:

bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING

From then on it lives the life of every key of the tenant, with the same commands: beffroi:keys:rotate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING stages a successor, beffroi:keys:activate brings a staged key in before its date, beffroi:keys:retire takes a retiring one out, and the timed step stages a successor on its own once the active key has worked its age.
